So this is not a quirk of one function - the lifter emits switch cases as unreachable blocks inside their owning function and never registers them as dispatchable, so EVERY indirect jump through a table fails and lands on whatever the ITAIL fallback does. Each failure strands the owning function's pushes, which is how it surfaces: a stack leak and a clobbered callee-saved register, far from the switch. DELIBERATELY NOT MASS-SEEDING. 2,651 seeds in one step is exactly the wide-scope change seed_missing_functions.py's docstring warns about, and the 2026-08-05 entry records a 25x regression (1452 -> 56) from batch-adding 13 unverified fragments. These targets are better founded than those were - they are read from real jump tables, so they are certainly real instruction starts - but each seeded fragment still runs from its address to the owner's end, duplicating tails, which is the exact mechanism of that regression. WHAT I DID INSTEAD: finished the one table proven to be on the boot path. Seeded the remaining four entries of 0x001F84AC (0x001F83EF, 0x001F83F6, 0x001F83FD, 0x001F8404) after 0x001F840B from #54. Deterministic 2 of 2: 82/3/22/8, reached still 54, crash unchanged. Neutral as expected - index 4 is the only one taken on this boot - but they are strictly more faithful and pre-empt the same failure the moment another index comes up. STAGED PLAN for the rest, in order of value: (1) when a wall involves a switch, check its table first - this sweep makes that a lookup; (2) seed per-table for tables owned by functions already on the boot path, measuring per table; (3) only consider a bulk pass once a per-table pass has shown it is safe, and back up seed_list.json first (the 2026-08-05 entry is explicit that this is what made recovery cheap). The sweep script is at scratchpad/sweep_jumptables.py and is worth promoting into tools_data/ - it is title-agnostic and re-runnable after any regeneration.

entries.claim: The faithful sweep does NOT yield a backlog of deferred-flag bugs. Its 1094 findings are dominated by unlifted stubs, and its flag column produces false positives; the accurate detector reports ZERO remaining sites. The class is clean
entries.evidence: Ran `faithful --sweep 0` as planned: 30,002 functions checked, 1,094 with findings. THREE LAYERS OF INFLATION, peeled one at a time. (1) The ranking is by missing labels weighted 10x, and almost every top scorer lives in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c - sub_000C2145 with 170 "missing labels", sub_0006129A with 121, and so on. A stub has no labels because it was never lifted, so those rows re-report the missing-function class, not a miscompile. (2) Filtering to the flags column in LIFTED code only gives 835 functions - but those collapse to 329 DISTINCT sites, because heavily overlapping fragments report the same site repeatedly (sub_002106B0 and sub_00210710 both report the identical two entries). (3) Of those 329, re-checking each against the real file text rather than the body faithful was handed shows 34 already carry an `_sf` snapshot repair, leaving 295 claimed. THE 295 ARE FALSE POSITIVES. Hand-checked recomp_0000.c:2871, reported as "test esi, esi then pop esi" in sub_000125B0. The actual generated C is `esi = MEM32(eax + ecx * 4 + 4); (void)0; /* test esi, esi - flags set */; PUSH32(esp, edi); if (TEST_Z(esi, esi)) goto ...` - the intervening instruction PUSHES EDI and never touches esi. faithful matched a `pop esi` that occurs elsewhere in the original x86, not between the test and the branch. CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY by the project's own purpose-built pair: find_stale_flag_tests.py scans 15,234 deferred-flag sites and reports "sites whose tested register is clobbered: 0", and fix_stale_flags.py answers "nothing to fix - already applied, or the detector reports none". Those two work from the generated C, which is the thing that actually runs, so they cannot be fooled by instruction pairing across branches the way the disassembly-side check can. CONCLUSION: the deferred-flag class is CLEAN. The one real instance (0x001F0AB2, ledger #44, worth reached 37 -> 43) was found and fixed today, and faithful DID name it correctly - so the checker is still valuable per-function, where its output is read with the source in front of you. It is its SWEEP mode that should not be treated as a work queue. PRACTICAL UPSHOT, and the reason this is worth recording as a refutation rather than a note: without this check the obvious next move was to work through 295 "known bugs", every one of which would have cost a build, a run and a hand inspection to disprove. Use find_stale_flag_tests.py for this class, not the faithful sweep. Tree unchanged by this investigation: 82/3/22/8 deterministic, reached 54.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to #55: the jump-table problem is 75 tables / 608 targets, not 265 / 2,651. The _jt dispatch form is SAFE and must not be counted, and seeded functions register in recomp_manual.c not recomp_dispatch.c. Zero remain on the boot path - that work is DONE
entries.evidence: Went to seed the boot-path tables and found my own sweep was wrong in two ways, both of which inflated it. ERROR 1 - THE SAFE FORM WAS COUNTED. The lifter emits two shapes. The bare `RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE))` is the broken one (ledger #54). The other is `{ uint32_t _jt = MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE); if (_jt == 0x002164CDu) goto loc_002164CD; ... RECOMP_ITAIL(_jt); }` - every target resolved inline by an explicit goto, with the ITAIL only a fallback. That form is FINE. Verified by reading sub_0021624C's table 0x00216590, which my sweep had flagged as "8/8 missing" while the generated C resolves all six distinct targets by goto. Counting it took the site count from 83 to 272. ERROR 2 - THE WRONG REGISTRY WAS CHECKED. seed_missing_functions.py registers through `recomp_lookup_manual()` in src/recomp_manual.c as `if (xbox_va == 0x001F840Bu) return sub_001F840B;`, NOT in recomp_dispatch.c. My sweep only read the dispatch table, so it reported the seven targets I had already seeded as still missing. CORRECTED FIGURES: 83 bare-ITAIL sites, 75 tables with unregistered targets, 608 distinct targets. Ledger #55's "265 tables / 2,651 targets" is withdrawn. THE BOOT-PATH WORK IS ALREADY COMPLETE. Checked all 20 functions in the current crash backtrace and the chains confirmed executing this session against the corrected sweep: ZERO have an unregistered bare-ITAIL table. sub_001F83D0's table 0x001F84AC was the only one on the path and all seven of its targets are seeded (0x001F840B in #54, then 0x001F83EF/F6/FD, 0x001F8404, 0x001F8443, 0x001F844A). The two tables that looked like boot-path hits, in sub_0021624C and sub_0021644B, are both the safe _jt form. So there is nothing further to seed here right now - the remaining 608 targets are all in functions the boot does not currently reach, and will become relevant as it gets further. TOOL FIXED AND KEPT: tools_data/sweep_jumptables.py now matches only the bare form, unions recomp_dispatch.c with recomp_manual.c, takes --func to check one function, and documents both mistakes in its header so they are not repeated. Re-run it after any regeneration or whenever a new wall involves a switch. Signals unchanged throughout: 82/3/22/8 deterministic, reached 54.

entries.claim: The 0xFFFFFFFD crash is in sub_002053F0, NOT sub_00205170 - triage mis-attributed it again. Also seeded sub_001ECAD0, a newly-reached missing function: reached 54 -> 55, failed icalls 3 -> 2
entries.evidence: TWO RESULTS, one a fix and one a correction. THE SEED: the failed-icall list changed after the jump-table fix (#54) from the usual 0x1/0x0 garbage to include 0x001ECAD0, a real-looking .text address - a sign we now reach code that calls it. sub_001ECAD0 appears NOWHERE in the tree: not lifted, not in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c, not referenced by any generated line, so it is reached purely through a function pointer. Seeded it (17 bytes, 0x001ECAD0-0x001ECAE1). Deterministic 2 of 2: reached 54 -> 55, failed_icalls 3 -> 2, kernel_calls and heap_allocs unchanged at 82 and 22. A small but real gain, and it confirms the pattern that a failed icall to a plausible .text address is a genuinely missing function worth seeding. It did NOT move the crash, so it is not the cause of this wall. THE CORRECTION, and this is the more important half: triage reports the crash as sub_00205170+0x6F3, but resolving RVA 0xDFC7B3 against the linker map puts it inside sub_002053F0, which spans 0xDFBD00-0xDFC820. The symbols either side are sub_002053CC at 0xDFBC60 and sub_0020563B at 0xDFC820, so the attribution is unambiguous. triage is using a symbol source that lacks sub_002053F0 (seeded_functions.json rather than the linker map) and therefore falls back to the nearest name it does know. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME TODAY - ledger #48 lost a full turn to exactly this, when a divide was attributed to sub_001FAB40 while the code belonged to sub_001FA9E0. The lesson from #48 should have been applied here immediately: when chasing a crash, resolve the RVA against build/*.map yourself before deep-diving whatever triage names. CONSEQUENCE: ledgers #45 and #46 deep-dived sub_00205170 for the EARLIER crashes at +0x5EA and 0xD8282444 and their findings about the coalescer stand on their own probe evidence, but the CURRENT wall was never in that function. sub_002053F0 is fresh ground - faithful is CLEAN on it (149 insns, ratio 1.28, no missing labels, no stale flags), it has no ledger history, its only caller is a fall-through from sub_002053CC, and it reads globals 0x5BC508 and 0x5BC5D8 with one ICALL through MEM32(edi + 0x98). STILL OPEN: which read produces 0xFFFFFFFD. Registers are eax=5 ebx=0x2F000000 ecx=0 edx=0 edi=4 esi=1. The function has NO reads with a negative displacement, and its only two reads off the zero registers are MEM32(edx + 0x30) and MEM32(ecx + 0xC0), which would fault at 0x30 and 0xC0, not at -3. So the faulting address is computed, and the honest next step is to disassemble sub_002053F0 forward from 0xDFBD00 to the fault - the technique that cracked #48 - rather than guess from the register dump. Tree clean: no probes, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to my own #58: triage was RIGHT - the crash IS sub_00205170+0x6F3. I mis-parsed the linker map, reading the section-relative column as an RVA. The faulting instruction is the backward-coalescing footer read MEM32(esi + -4) with esi = 1
entries.evidence: MY #58 CORRECTION WAS ITSELF WRONG AND MUST NOT BE ACTED ON. The MSVC map has three address columns per row: `0001:00dfbd00  sub_002053F0  0000000140dfcd00 f  recomp_0015.c.obj`. The first is SECTION-RELATIVE, the third is Rva+Base with image base 0x140000000. I parsed the first as an RVA, which is off by the section VA, and that shifted every lookup. Re-resolved with the correct column (62,972 symbols): fault RVA 0xDFC7B3 -> sub_00205170 + 0x6F3, symbol at 0xDFC0C0. That is EXACTLY what triage said. sub_002053F0 is at 0xDFCD00, well past the fault. RE-CHECKED #48 THE SAME WAY, because it made the mirror-image claim: RVA 0xDAEB5D -> sub_001FA9E0 + 0x15D (symbol 0xDAEA00), while sub_001FAB40 sits at 0xDAF3A0. So #48's CONCLUSION was right - the divide really is in sub_001FA9E0, which idiom-matching had already established - but triage was genuinely wrong there while being right here. So triage is not reliably wrong; it is inconsistent. The durable rule is simply: resolve against the Rva+Base column yourself, which is authoritative either way. THE ACTUAL ANSWER, obtained by disassembling from the correct base 0xDFC0C0 (435 instructions, target on a clean boundary): 0x00DFC7B0 `lea ecx, [rdx - 4]` then 0x00DFC7B3 `mov edx, dword ptr [rcx + rax]` where rax holds the guest memory base loaded from [rip + 0x9be610]. So the faulting expression is MEM32(guest_reg - 4) and the guest register is 1, giving 1 - 4 = 0xFFFFFFFD exactly as reported. In the generated C that is `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)` at loc_00205276 - the BACKWARD-COALESCING FOOTER READ, corroborated by deepdive's field list for sub_00205170 which shows esi with a -0x4 read and nothing else negative. SO WE ARE BACK IN THE COALESCER of ledgers #45/#46, one layer on: the walk now reaches loc_00205276 with esi = 1 instead of a block pointer, reads the previous block's footer at esi-4, and faults. Previously the bad value was a vtable pointer (#45) and then the walk was fixed by seeding (#46); now it is the small integer 1, which is the same signature as the switch index 4 that ledger #54 traced to a stranded jump-table push. NEXT STEP: probe esi at loc_002051D0 and loc_00205276 to see where the 1 enters the walk, and check whether it arrives from the deferred-free array or from a register clobbered across one of the loop's calls - both have precedent today. Tree clean: no probes, 82/2/22/8 deterministic, reached 55.

entries.claim: The 0xFFFFFFFD crash is an ALIASING bug: sub_00211280 decrements a refcount at MEM32(obj + 4) where obj = MEM32(esi + 0xB0) resolves to the POOL 0x011CE000, and pool+4 is simultaneously the first slot of the deferred-free array sub_00205170 walks. The refcount value 1 is then read as a block pointer
entries.evidence: Traced the fault end to end. THE FAULTING INSTRUCTION, from disassembling sub_00205170 at its true base 0xDFC0C0: `0x00DFC7B0 lea ecx, [rdx - 4]` then `0x00DFC7B3 mov edx, dword ptr [rcx + rax]` with rax the guest base - i.e. the generated `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)` at loc_00205276, the backward-coalescing footer read, with esi = 1 giving MEM32(0xFFFFFFFD). WHERE THE 1 COMES FROM, probed at three points in the walk with a limit high enough not to truncate (the first attempt capped at 12 and hid it): the deferred-free array walks cleanly for several passes - cursor 0x011CE004 through 0x011CE020 with entries null except a valid block 0x011D0004 at 0x011CE008 - and then on a later pass `[W:LIST] cursor=0x011CE004 entry=0x00000001`. The SLOT ITSELF changed from 0 to 1 between passes. Confirmed downstream: `[W:HDR] esi=0x00000001 hdr=0x2F000000`, and LO8(0x2F000000) = 0 so the PREV_INUSE bit is clear and the code takes the backward-merge path exactly as in #45. hdr also matches ebx=0x2F000000 in the crash dump. THE WRITER, from a write-watch on 0x011CE004: RIP RVA 0xE4D125 = sub_00211280 + 0x365 (resolved with the Rva+Base column per #59). sub_00211280 is faithful-CLEAN (118 insns, ratio 1.23). Its two writes to +4 are the same idiom: `ecx = MEM32(esi + 0xB0); if (ecx == ebx) skip; edx = MEM32(ecx + 4); edx--; MEM32(ecx + 4) = edx; if (eax & 0x7FFFFF) skip;` - a REFERENCE-COUNT DECREMENT with the same 0x7FFFFF mask seen in sub_00011B35. So the value 1 is a refcount, not a pointer. THE CONFLICT: sub_00211280 treats MEM32(pool + 4) as a refcount field on the object at MEM32(esi + 0xB0), while sub_00205170 treats MEM32(pool + 4) as the FIRST SLOT of the deferred-free array - and #46 verified that array reading works, since slot pool+8 legitimately held the valid block 0x011D0004. Both cannot be right about the same four bytes. NOT YET PROVEN, and this is the fork: either MEM32(esi + 0xB0) wrongly holds the pool pointer when it should point at some refcounted object, or the array base is off by one slot. The cheap decisive test is to probe esi and MEM32(esi + 0xB0) at loc_0021133E and loc_00211369 and see whether that field is meant to be the pool at all - if it is a stale or mis-assigned pointer, the aliasing is the bug; if it legitimately IS the pool, then the pool genuinely carries a refcount at +4 and sub_00205170's array must start at +8. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic, reached 55.

entries.claim: The current wall is sub_00205170+0x682 (fault 0xB0348CB9), NOT the +0x6F3 / 0xFFFFFFFD read that ledger #60 analysed. Same function, 0x71 apart, different read. Re-baseline before acting on #60
entries.evidence: Checked determinism after noticing the possibility tool's baseline crash did not match my earlier measurement. Per-build determinism is FINE: 4 of 4 runs give exactly RVA=0xDFC742, all four counters identical, verdict deterministic. Tree integrity also verified - zero probe lines left in gen/, all four of today's seeds still registered in recomp_manual.c (sub_001F840B, sub_001ECAD0, sub_001E6CC9, sub_001E6C5B), and the deferred-flag manual fix still present in recomp_0014.c. So this is not a dirty tree and not run-to-run noise. BUT THE WALL MOVED between measurements. Resolved both addresses against the Rva+Base column: 0xDFC7B3 = sub_00205170 + 0x6F3 and 0xDFC742 = sub_00205170 + 0x682. Same function, 0x71 apart, but the fault address differs completely - 0x10000FFFD (guest 0xFFFFFFFD, the esi-4 footer read with esi=1) versus 0xB0348CB9 (guest ~0xB0338CB9, wild garbage). Those are DIFFERENT reads in the same coalescer loop. I cannot cleanly attribute the shift. The +0x6F3 measurement was taken probe-free right after seeding sub_001ECAD0; the current one is probe-free too. Candidates: the possibility tool builds via build_compile.bat directly while the MCP build may take another path, or a probe/strip cycle changed layout - ledger #17 already refuted "probes are behaviourally free". Not worth chasing on its own; what matters is the consequence. CONSEQUENCE, and this is why it is recorded rather than shrugged off: ledger #60's whole analysis - the refcount/array aliasing at pool+4, the write-watch, the sub_00211280 attribution - was of the +0x6F3 read. It is sound for THAT read but is NOT established as the cause of the wall standing in front of us now. The possibility run is still informative: variant A (suppress the refcount store to the pool) MOVED the crash while variant B (shift the array base to +8) was completely inert, so the aliasing is real and the array base is not the problem. But neither improved reached, and A merely moved the crash to the +0x6F3 read - i.e. A converts the current wall into the previously-analysed one. NEXT STEP: re-triage the CURRENT crash at +0x682 from scratch - resolve the faulting instruction by disassembling from sub_00205170's true base and read what it dereferences - before spending anything further on #60. Two turns were already lost today to acting on a mis-identified location.

entries.claim: RESOLVES #61: +0x682 and +0x6F3 are ONE bug, not two. Both consume esi = 1 from the corrupted deferred-free slot at pool+4; which garbage read faults first depends only on code layout. Ledger #60's analysis DOES apply to the live wall
entries.evidence: Re-triaged +0x682 from scratch as planned. THE FAULTING INSTRUCTION, disassembled from sub_00205170's true base 0xDFC0C0 (406 insns, clean boundary): `0x00DFC733 mov rax, [rip + 0x9be686]` loads the guest memory base, `0x00DFC73E add ecx, [r12 + r14]` computes block + size, then `0x00DFC742 mov edx, [rcx + rax]` faults - and the next instructions are `mov eax, edx; shr eax, 5`, the 19-bit size unpack seen throughout this allocator. So +0x682 is the FORWARD walk `edx = MEM32(edi + esi)`: step to the next block and read its header. +0x6F3, analysed in #60, is the BACKWARD merge `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)`. Different reads, same loop. THEY SHARE ONE CAUSE. Probed the walk with a limit high enough not to truncate: [S:LIST] cursor=0x011CE004 entry=0x00000001, then [S:BLK] esi=0x00000001 hdr=0x2F000000, then [S:NEXT] esi=0x00000001 ebx=0x2F000000. That is the SAME corrupted array slot #60 traced to sub_00211280's refcount decrement, and the same header 0x2F000000 read out of guest low memory at MEM32(1). With esi = 1 the unpacked size is garbage, so `edi + esi` is garbage and the forward read faults; on a different layout the backward read faults first instead. CONFIRMED BY THE FLIP: stripping the probes moved the crash back from 0xDFC742 (+0x682) to 0xDFC7B3 (+0x6F3), deterministic 2 of 2 either way. The wall did not change between measurements - the same corruption simply exits through whichever garbage read the code layout puts first. That fully explains the "wall moved" puzzle in #61, which is now closed. So #60 stands and is live: the deferred-free slot at pool+4 is written with a refcount by sub_00211280 and read as a block pointer by sub_00205170. CAVEAT ON THE POSSIBILITY RUN: variant A guarded its store with `ecx != MEM32(MEM32(0x5BC508) + 0x70)`, but there are TWO pools in play - 0x01089A90 and 0x011CE000, both seen taking `[7DC:W1] writing 0x00001000` - so that guard may have protected the wrong one and A's apparent "crash moved" is likely just the same layout flip, not a real effect. Re-run the possibility spec with the guard keyed to the pool the walk actually uses (0x011CE000, i.e. whichever MEM32(manager+0x70) the failing walk holds) before drawing anything from A vs B. NEXT STEP: re-arm the write-watch on 0x011CE004 to confirm sub_00211280 is still the writer on the current build, then decide between "esi+0xB0 holds the wrong object" and "the pool legitimately has a refcount at +4" with a variant that targets the right pool. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: RETRACTS #60: the write-watch caught the pool CONSTRUCTOR zeroing itself (a 517-dword rep stosd writing 0), not a refcount decrement. The watch is ONE-SHOT and disarmed on that first legitimate write, so the actual writer of the value 1 into pool+4 was never seen and is still unknown
entries.evidence: Re-armed the watch on 0x011CE004 as planned. It fired again at the same RIP, RVA 0xE4D125 = sub_00211280 + 0x365 (resolved via Rva+Base). But disassembling sub_00211280 from its true base 0xE4CDC0 shows what that instruction actually is: `mov eax,[rbx+r9]; mov ecx,[rbx+rsi]; lea edx,[rax+r8*4]; inc r8d; mov [rdx+rax], ecx; cmp r8d, eax; jb` - an INDEXED FILL LOOP, not a refcount update. The matching C at recomp_0015.c:44505 is unambiguous: `edi = MEM32(esi + 0x70); eax = 0; ecx = 0x205; for (_i = 0; _i < ecx; _i++) MEM32(edi + _i*4) = eax;` - a lifted `rep stosd` zeroing 517 dwords (0x814 bytes) of the pool. It writes ZERO, and it is the pool constructor doing exactly what it should. WHY #60 WAS WRONG: I assumed the first watched write was the corrupting one. It was not - it is the earliest write to that address in the boot, which is the memset, and the watch DISARMS after one hit ("Each fires once, names the writing instruction, then disarms"). Everything after it, including whatever actually stores 1, went unobserved. CORROBORATED by probing the two refcount sites I had blamed: [RC1] at loc_0021133E gives esi=011CD000 objB0=0x00000018 ecx=0x18, and [RC2] at loc_00211369 gives obj78=0x00000018 ecx=0x18. MEM32(manager+0xB0) and MEM32(manager+0x78) both hold 0x18 - not pointers - so both sites decrement MEM32(0x1C) in guest low memory, nowhere near the pool. They cannot be the writer. The refcount/array ALIASING story in #60 is therefore withdrawn entirely. ALSO INVALIDATES the possibility run: [RC1] shows g508pool = MEM32(MEM32(0x5BC508) + 0x70) = 0x00000000, so variant A's guard `ecx != MEM32(MEM32(0x5BC508) + 0x70)` compared against ZERO and could never fire. A was a no-op, and its "crash MOVED" was the layout flip of #62, exactly as that entry cautioned. Variant B being inert remains the only real signal from that run. WHAT STANDS: the fault itself (#62) - both +0x682 and +0x6F3 consume esi = 1 taken from the deferred-free slot at 0x011CE004, measured directly. What is unknown again is who writes the 1. TOOL LIMITATION WORTH REMEMBERING: a one-shot write-watch answers "what wrote here FIRST", which is only the same question as "what corrupted this" when the address starts out untouched. Here the constructor writes it legitimately first. NEXT STEP: bracket the write in time instead - probe MEM32(0x011CE004) at the entry of several functions on the boot path (sub_00211280, sub_0020A8B0, sub_00205170) and find the first point where it already reads 1; that narrows the window without needing a re-arming watch. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: The 1 is written by sub_001F7CD0+0x8A - a C++ CONSTRUCTOR (stores vtable 0x3EEAE8 at +0 and refcount 1 at +4) running on 0x011CE000, the exact address sub_00205170 walks as its deferred-free array. An object is being constructed on top of the live pool
entries.evidence: Bracketed the write in time first: canaries at the entry of 17 boot-path functions put it between sub_001FA9E0 (slot still 0) and sub_00202B87 (slot already 1). The window contained only kernel calls - NtQueryVirtualMemory, NtFreeVirtualMemory, and Enter/LeaveCriticalSection pairs - and none of those bridges can be responsible: bridge_NtFreeVirtualMemory is a pure no-op, and xbox_RtlEnterCriticalSection keeps its state in a SIDE TABLE keyed by address (cs_slot_for) and never writes the guest structure. So the writer was game code inside the window, which the canaries did not cover. THE TOOL I SHOULD HAVE USED FIRST: main.c already implements RECOMP_WATCH_TRACE=<n>, which reports EVERY write with its value and never disarms. Its own docstring states the exact lesson #63 relearned the hard way - "without it a watch answers who wrote here FIRST, and that turned out to be the wrong question every single time on 2026-08-06". It is not wired into the MCP run tool (which only sets RECOMP_WATCH), so it has to be set in the same cmd that launches the exe - a bat wrapper works, `cmd /c` from git-bash does not pass it through. FULL WRITE HISTORY of 0x011CE004, resolved against Rva+Base: #1 = 0x00000000 from sub_00211280+0x3B5 (the pool constructor's 517-dword rep stosd, the write that the one-shot watch wasted itself on); #2 = 0x00000001 from sub_001F7CD0+0x8A; #3 and #4 write byte +0x3 from the same function; #5 = 0x00000001 again from sub_00202C70+0xD2; #7 = 0x00000000 from sub_00205170+0x5D1, which is the consumer clearing the slot at loc_002051DA exactly as it should. THE WRITER IS A CONSTRUCTOR. sub_001F7CD0 is 56 lines and its body is unmistakable: `esi = ecx; eax = MEM32(esi+4); eax &= 0xFF000001; eax |= 1; MEM32(esi+4) = eax; MEM32(esi) = 0x3EEAE8; MEM8(esi+7) = 0;` - a vtable pointer stored at +0 and a refcount initialised to 1 at +4, the standard shape, and it has 16 callers across the tree. So `this` = 0x011CE000 and the object's refcount field IS the four bytes sub_00205170 reads as its first array slot. CONCLUSION: an object is being constructed ON TOP OF the live pool. The coalescer then reads the refcount 1 as a block pointer, and both crash sites in #62 follow from that. This is the aliasing #60 suspected but attributed to the wrong writer. STILL OPEN: why the two overlap. Either the engine's pool bookkeeping hands 0x011CE000 out for an object while it is still in use as a pool, or MEM32(manager + 0x70) is stale and points at memory that has legitimately been recycled. Note the pool control word was 0x0000004B when the walk read it (#46) and the constructor stores 0x3EEAE8 at +0, so reading MEM32(0x011CE000) at the crash would say which owner won - that is the next single measurement. Tree clean: 54 canary lines stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: The object wins: MEM32(0x011CE000) changes from the pool control word 0x49 to a VTABLE 0x003EEF28 BETWEEN two steps of the same walk. The pool is being recycled into a C++ object while sub_00205170 is still iterating it - a use-after-free in the engine's own allocator, not a lifting bug
entries.evidence: Read MEM32(0x011CE000) at each step of the failing walk, as planned. Two steps, and they disagree about what lives there: [OWNER] esi=011D0004 word0=0x00000049 slot4=0x00000000 - the pool control word, intact, matching the 0x4B/count-9 shape #46 measured; then [OWNER] esi=0x00000001 word0=0x003EEF28 slot4=0x00000000 - word0 is now a VTABLE POINTER, in the same .rdata vtable region as the 0x3EEAE8 that sub_001F7CD0's constructor stores and the 0x3EECB0 and 0x3F4770 vtables probed all session. So the pool header is overwritten by an object BETWEEN two iterations of one walk. That settles #64's open question: the object owner wins, and the overlap is not a stale pointer being read - it is live memory being taken out from under an in-progress iteration. THE SHAPE IS A USE-AFTER-FREE. sub_00205170 holds a pointer to the pool at 0x011CE000, walks its deferred-free array, and part-way through that walk the engine constructs a refcounted C++ object at the same address - sub_001F7CD0 storing a vtable at +0 and refcount 1 at +4 (#64), with a second constructor evidently running after it since the final vtable is 0x3EEF28 rather than 0x3EEAE8. The walk then reads the refcount as its next array entry, gets 1, and dies on either MEM32(esi-4) or MEM32(edi+esi) depending on layout (#62). NOTE WHAT THIS IS NOT. Our xbox_HeapAlloc is bump-only and never reuses an address (#29's caveat: RtlFreeHeap is a leak), so the recycling cannot come from the port's allocator. It has to be the ENGINE's own allocator handing 0x011CE000 back out - which means the engine believes that memory is free while a walk over it is still running. Every lifting-level explanation is therefore excluded, and so is a fix in the bridge or the lifter: this is engine bookkeeping, reached only because the earlier fixes (#35, #44, #46, #54) got the allocator far enough to start recycling at all. NEXT STEP: find what frees the pool. The engine must return 0x011CE000 to its own free list shortly before the constructor runs; a RECOMP_WATCH_TRACE on 0x011CE000 itself (not +4) will show every writer of the header in order, and the write that precedes the vtable store is the free. Use trace mode from the start - the one-shot watch cost two turns on this address already (#63). Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: Full ownership history of the pool header traced: sub_00222628+0x127 calls constructor sub_00202C70 with this = 0x011CE000 while MEM32(0x011CE000) still reads the LIVE pool control word 0x49. There is no free marker - the pool is simply built over
entries.evidence: Ran RECOMP_WATCH_TRACE=60 on 0x011CE000 (the header, not +4) via a bat wrapper - the env does not survive `cmd /c` from git-bash, so it must be set in the same cmd that launches the exe. ELEVEN WRITES, resolved against Rva+Base, in order: #1 = 0 from RVA 0x37F41E75B (outside the module - a system DLL memset); #2 = 0 from sub_00211280+0x365, the pool's own 517-dword rep stosd; #3 = 0x48 from sub_00204BD0+0x2A1; #4 = 0x4B from sub_0020AA90+0xE59; #5, #6, #7 = 0x49 from sub_00205170+0x4CD - the WALK ITSELF maintaining the header, which is normal coalescer bookkeeping; then #8 = 0x003EEAE8 from sub_001F7CD0+0x98, #9 = 0x003EEED0 from sub_00202C70+0xF6, #10 = 0x003EEF28 from sub_00202C70+0x2F1 - three vtable stores in sequence, the signature of a THREE-LEVEL C++ class hierarchy being constructed; and finally #11 = 0x003EEF28 from sub_00205170+0x4CD, the walk writing the vtable value back as if it were a block header, which is the corruption propagating. CRITICALLY, THERE IS NO FREE BETWEEN #7 AND #8. The header goes straight from 0x49 (live pool) to a vtable. Nothing marks the memory as released, so whatever recycled it did not go through the header at all - the engine's free bookkeeping lives elsewhere, or there was no free. THE CALLER, from a recomp_where probe at sub_00202C70's entry: [CTOR] this=0x011CE000 hdr=0x00000049, reached via sub_00222628+0x127 <- sub_00236500+0x594 <- sub_00239E50 <- sub_00011E40, under bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx. So sub_00222628 hands the constructor the pool's address WHILE THE HEADER STILL READS 0x49 - the object is built on memory the pool believes it owns, during engine startup. WHERE THIS LANDS: our xbox_HeapAlloc is bump-only and cannot hand the same address out twice (#29), so this is not the port's allocator. Either the ENGINE's allocator returned 0x011CE000 for this construction, or sub_00222628 obtained the address by reading a field that happens to hold the pool pointer - a placement-new onto the wrong buffer. Those are distinguishable and it is the last hop: probe sub_00222628 around its call site at +0x127 and see where the `this` it passes comes from - an allocation return value, or a struct field read. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: ROOT CAUSE REACHED: the `this` is an ALLOCATION RETURN VALUE. sub_00222628 calls the engine allocator sub_001F7E00 for 0x10 bytes and gets back 0x011CE000 - the live pool - then constructs a C++ object on it. The engine allocator is handing out memory it is still using
entries.evidence: Read sub_00222628 (53 lines, recomp_0016.c:18545) and the answer is in its first eight lines, no probe needed: `edx = MEM32(esp + 4); PUSH esi; PUSH edx; PUSH 0; PUSH 0x10; call sub_001F7E00;` then `esp = esp + 0xC; if (eax == 0) goto sub_0022265D;` - a null check, which is what an allocation return looks like - then `PUSH 1; ecx = eax; call sub_00202C70`. So `this` is NOT a struct field read and NOT a placement-new onto a passed-in buffer: it is the RETURN VALUE of sub_001F7E00 called with size 0x10. #66 posed those two possibilities; it is the first one. THE COMPLETE CHAIN, every link measured this session: sub_001F7E00 allocates 16 bytes and returns 0x011CE000, which is MEM32(manager + 0x70) - the pool that sub_00205170 is at that moment walking, its header still reading the live control word 0x49 (#66). sub_00202C70 then constructs a three-level C++ object there, writing vtables 0x3EEAE8, 0x3EEED0 and 0x3EEF28 at +0 and a refcount of 1 at +4 (#64, #66). The in-progress walk reads +4 as its next deferred-free array slot, gets 1, and faults on either MEM32(esi-4) or MEM32(edi+esi) depending on code layout (#62). So the defect is that THE ENGINE ALLOCATOR RETURNS MEMORY THAT IS STILL IN USE. Not the port's allocator - xbox_HeapAlloc is bump-only and cannot repeat an address (#29) - and not a lifting bug, since faithful is clean on every function in this chain. IMPORTANT FRAMING: this is only reachable because the earlier fixes worked. The engine could not recycle anything until #35 made pool growth work, #44 got the region registrar running, #46 stopped a stack leak corrupting the walk, and #54 fixed the jump-table dispatch. A use-after-free in the engine's allocator is a much later-stage failure than anything seen before today. NEXT STEP: probe sub_001F7E00 - what does it return on each call, and does 0x011CE000 come off a free list or out of a fresh carve? If the pool was pushed onto the engine's own free list, find what freed it; the pool contains its deferred-free array at +4, so a self-referential free is plausible and would explain why no free marker was ever written to the header. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: The 16-byte allocation does NOT come from sub_003437F3 - it takes sub_001F7E00's early exit into sub_001F7E57, which allocates through the MANAGER's own vtable+0xCC. So the manager's pool allocator returned the pool's own base address, 0x011CE000, and the constructor then overwrote the pool header and first array slot
entries.evidence: Followed the allocation to its source. sub_001F7E00 reads size from esp+4 and a PREFIX size from esp+0x10 into edi, computes esi = size + edi, and then has THREE outcomes: two early exits to sub_001F7E57 (when the esp+0x14 argument is non-zero, and when an ICALL through MEM32(0x5BC5DC)'s vtable+0x58 returns non-zero), and only as a fallback does it call sub_003437F3. sub_001F7E57 is five lines: `edx = MEM32(eax); PUSH esi; ecx = eax; ICALL MEM32(edx + 0xCC);` then `eax = eax + edi` - allocate size+prefix through an allocator OBJECT's vtable+0xCC, then bias the result past the prefix. That is a standard allocate-with-header idiom, and vtable+0xCC on vtbl 0x003F4770 is sub_001EC5E0, the manager's allocate thunk identified in ledger #38. THE DECISIVE EVIDENCE that this is the path taken: sub_003437F3 carries PERMANENT instrumentation (a manual addition recording every returned pointer into g_alloc_trace, deliberately not marked /* PROBE */ so strip_probes leaves it), and its crash-time dump reads "Allocator returned 10 pointer(s)" listing 0x01082000, 0x01083000, 0x01085000, 0x01086000, 0x01087000, 0x01088A90, 0x01089A90, 0x011CD000, 0x011CE000, 0x01311000 - and explicitly "0 failed (returned NULL), 0 repeated a live address". So sub_003437F3 handed out 0x011CE000 EXACTLY ONCE and never repeated any address. The duplicate therefore cannot have come from it. Since sub_00222628's 16-byte request demonstrably returned 0x011CE000 (#67) and that value appears only once in the trace, the request must have gone down the untraced sub_001F7E57 path. CONCLUSION: the MANAGER'S OWN POOL ALLOCATOR returned the pool's base address. 0x011CE000 is MEM32(manager + 0x70) - the pool - with its control word at +0 and its deferred-free array at +4. Asked for 16 bytes, it handed back a block starting AT the pool base rather than at a carved block inside it, so the constructor's vtable store landed on the control word and its refcount on array slot 0. That is why no free marker was ever written (#66): nothing was freed. The pool allocator simply carved from the wrong offset. NOT YET CONFIRMED and worth one probe before acting: that vtable+0xCC on THIS object is sub_001EC5E0 (it is on vtbl 0x003F4770 per #38, but the allocator object here comes from MEM32(eax) at sub_001F7E57's entry and has not been identified for this call), and what edi (the prefix size) is - if edi is 0 the returned pointer is the raw block base, which would explain landing exactly on the pool base rather than a few bytes in. Probe sub_001F7E57's entry for eax, MEM32(eax), MEM32(MEM32(eax)+0xCC), esi and edi. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic, reached 55.

entries.claim: ROOT CAUSE of the sub_00205170 crash: the pool allocator sub_001EC5E0 returns NULL (a legitimate failure) but CLOBBERS callee-saved edi, leaving 0x011CE000 in it. sub_001F7E57's `eax = eax + edi` prefix bias then turns the NULL into 0x011CE000 - the pool's own base - so the caller's null check passes and the constructor overwrites the pool header. Callee-saved-clobber class, same as sub_001FAB40 losing esi (#52)
entries.evidence: MEASURED, two probe lines, deterministic build (82 kernel calls / 2 failed icalls / 22 heap allocs / 8 safe stubs, reached 55). Probes on both ends of sub_001F7E57, the untraced allocation path identified in #68: "[A:ENT] obj=0x01088A90 vtbl=0x003F4770 target=0x001EC5E0 size=0x00000010 edi=0x00000000" and "[A:RET] raw=0x00000000 edi=0x011CE000 -> 0x011CE000". Exactly one allocation takes this path all boot. THREE facts, each read directly: (1) The ICALL target IS sub_001EC5E0 on vtbl 0x003F4770, confirming ledger #38's identification for this call site - that was an assumption in #68 and is now measured. (2) The allocator RETURNED NULL. raw eax = 0x00000000. Asking the pool for 16 bytes FAILED. That failure is honest and sub_00222628 is written to handle it - it does `if (TEST_Z(eax, eax))` immediately on return (#67). (3) edi entered sub_001F7E57 as 0x00000000 and left the ICALL as 0x011CE000. edi is CALLEE-SAVED on x86, so sub_001EC5E0 is required to restore it; because the registers are C globals in the lifted tree, a callee that fails to restore one silently rewrites its caller's value. THE MECHANISM, end to end: sub_001F7E00 computes esi = size + prefix and puts the prefix in edi (here prefix = 0, so edi = 0). It tail-jumps to sub_001F7E57, which allocates size+prefix through the object's vtable+0xCC and then biases the result past the prefix with `eax = eax + edi`. With edi correctly preserved at 0 the arithmetic is 0 + 0 = 0, sub_00222628's null check fires, and the boot takes the allocation-failure path - faithful behaviour. With edi clobbered to 0x011CE000 the arithmetic is 0 + 0x011CE000 = 0x011CE000, the null check PASSES, and sub_00222628 hands that address to the constructor as `this`. sub_001F7CD0 then writes vtable 0x3EEAE8 to MEM32(this) and refcount 1 to MEM32(this + 4). But 0x011CE000 is MEM32(manager + 0x70) - the live pool - whose control word is at +0 and whose deferred-free array starts at +4. So the vtable store lands on the pool control word and the refcount 1 lands on array slot 0. That is the 1 at 0x011CE004 the trace-watch caught (#65), and it is why no free marker was ever written (#66): nothing was freed, and nothing was allocated either. sub_00205170 then reads the array, takes esi = 1, and either walks to MEM32(edi + 1) at +0x682 or reads the footer MEM32(1 - 4) = MEM32(0xFFFFFFFD) at +0x6F3 - the two faces of one bug (#62), which is why the site flips on layout changes. This closes the chain from the crash back to a single lifter defect. NEXT STEP: find where inside sub_001EC5E0 (or one of its callees) edi is lost, and fix the preservation - not the arithmetic in sub_001F7E57, which is a faithful lift. Run faithful on sub_001EC5E0 first; #46 showed the loss is more often in a callee than in the named function. SEPARATE QUESTION, do not conflate: WHY the pool allocator fails to serve 16 bytes at all. Fixing edi makes the boot take the honest failure path, which may surface as a clean out-of-memory rather than progress - the same shape as #40. Both want fixing; the clobber first, because it is corrupting memory.

entries.claim: The edi clobber of #69 IS the 40-byte stack leak of #39 - one and the same defect. This RETRACTS #40's decision not to fix it: the leak does not merely strand stack inside a fatal OOM reporter, it makes every caller's POP restore callee-saved registers from the wrong slot, and that is what corrupts the pool and causes the current crash. Fixing the 40 bytes is the fix for the wall
entries.evidence: MEASURED by walking edi and g_esp together down the allocator chain with entry + every-return-site probes (31 points across sub_001EC5E0, sub_00211530, sub_0020F860, sub_0020EFD0, sub_0020F209, sub_0020F0B2), each site with its OWN counter. Deterministic build 82/2/22/8, crash unchanged at RVA 0xDFC7B3. THE CONTROL, from the same run - a healthy sub_0020F860 call: "IN edi=0x00000010 esp=0x00F7FE90" and "R3 edi=0x00000010 esp=0x00F7FE90". esp restored exactly, edi preserved exactly. That is what a correct call looks like, and most calls in the log do this. THE FAILING CALL, the one feeding sub_001F7E57: "IN edi=0x00000010 esp=0x00F7FEAC" then "R4 edi=0x011CE000 esp=0x00F7FE84". 0x00F7FEAC - 0x00F7FE84 = 0x28 = 40 BYTES, and edi comes back as the pool pointer. THE SAME 40 BYTES RIDES ALL THE WAY OUT, every level inheriting it: sub_00211530 IN 0x00F7FEEC -> R5 0x00F7FEC4 (-0x28, edi=0x011CE000); sub_001EC5E0 IN 0x00F7FEFC -> R0 0x00F7FED4 (-0x28, edi=0x011CE000). sub_001EC5E0 then returns to sub_001F7E57, where `eax = eax + edi` adds that 0x011CE000 to a NULL allocation. WHERE THE 40 GOES, unchanged from #39: sub_0020F860 IN 0x00F7FEAC -> sub_0020EFD0 IN 0x00F7FE74 -> sub_0020EFD0 R0 (its tail-jump) 0x00F7FE34, a 0x40 drop that exactly matches the 64-byte frame sub_0020EFD0 allocates, so that function is CORRECT -> sub_0020F209 IN 0x00F7FE34 -> sub_0020F209 R7 (the full epilogue) 0x00F7FE4C. R7 unwound only 0x18 of the 0x40 it owes; 0x00F7FE74 was due, so it is short by exactly 0x28. And the register proves the pops read the wrong slots: edi at R7 is 0x00F7FE1C, a STACK ADDRESS, not any plausible saved value. sub_0020F860's own epilogue then pops ITS edi from a slot 40 bytes off and gets 0x011CE000. This is precisely #38's finding ("the stack is 40 bytes too deep at its epilogue, so POP32 reads uninitialised stack instead of the saved esi") reproduced on edi, one caller further out. WHY THIS RETRACTS #40: #40 refused the fix on the grounds that the leak lives inside the game's fatal out-of-memory reporter, which ends in `goto self` by design, so "repairing it buys a clean hang, not progress". The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The reporter path IS being taken - the pool allocator genuinely fails to serve 16 bytes and returns NULL - but the path RETURNS rather than hanging (R7, the balanced epilogue, is reached), and on the way out it destroys the callee-saved registers of four stacked callers. The damage is not confined to the reporter. It is what converts an honest allocation failure into a write through the pool's own base address, and thence to the sub_00205170 crash. So the leak must be fixed, and #40's "not worth fixing" no longer holds. NEXT STEP, unchanged from #39's open question and now worth doing: account for every push against every cleanup on sub_0020F209's path to its third sub_0020F0B2 tail-jump and find which 40 bytes are pushed without cleanup. The likely shape is arguments pushed for the two sub_001E8F30 calls or the vtable+0x54 ICALL whose cdecl cleanup (`esp + 8`, `esp + 0xC`, `esp + 0x14`) sits on a branch the retry path skips. SECOND, SEPARATE BUG still open and NOT to be conflated: why the pool allocator refuses a 16-byte request at all. Fixing the leak alone makes the boot take the honest failure branch in sub_00222628, which may read as a clean out-of-memory rather than as progress. Tree clean: 96 probe lines stripped, build verified.

entries.claim: THE 40 BYTES ARE FOUND, and they are TWO generic `g_esp += 4` stubs standing in for real code, not one leak: sub_001E9558 costs 8 bytes and sub_00011B2B costs 32. 8 + 32 = 40 exactly. Seeding both fragments is the fix for the current wall
entries.evidence: Answers #39's open question and completes #70. Method: bracket, then walk labels, then name the target - never guess. STEP 1, bracket to one call. The entry/return probes on sub_0020F209 fire BEFORE their return line, so they print on every pass and all three readings come from ONE invocation: IN esp=0x00F7FE34, R0 (loc_0020F480) 0x00F7FE34, R1 (loc_0020F491) 0x00F7FE34, R2 (loc_0020F4A7) 0x00F7FE0C. Balanced until R1, then 0x28 low at R2. Between loc_0020F491 and loc_0020F4A7 there is exactly ONE call: the ICALL through vtable+0x54. Probed it: "[V:PRE] slot54=0x001E8DB0 esp=0x00F7FE44" / "[V:POST] esp=0x00F7FE1C" and again "[V:PRE] esp=0x00F7FE34" / "[V:POST] esp=0x00F7FE0C" - sub_001E8DB0, minus 0x28 both times. STEP 2, walk every label in the reporter chain (85 probes across sub_001E8DB0, sub_00011A60, sub_00011AAE, sub_00011AB4, sub_00011B35), per-label counters. Baseline after sub_001E8DB0's 4 pushes is 0x00F7FE28. Readings: loc_00011A92 0x00F7FE10 (-24, the SEH frame, correct); loc_00011AC1 0x00F7FE10 (still correct); loc_00011ACD 0x00F7FDFC where 0x00F7FE04 was due - 8 BYTES GONE across sub_001E9C10; then loc_00011AD8, AE0, AEA, AF5, AFA, B09, B11, B1B ALL land exactly where the pushes and cleanups predict, so nothing else leaks; and then loc_001E8DC6 0x00F7FE04, meaning the chain RETURNED FROM loc_00011B1B and never reached sub_00011B35 at all. STEP 3, name both. (a) loc_00011B1B branches to sub_00011B2B, and recomp_stubs_unresolved.c:32 reads `void sub_00011B2B(void) { g_esp += 4; /* 0x00011B2B: not detected */ }`. The real code there falls into the SEH teardown at loc_00011C3F, which does POP esi + POP ebx + `esp + 0x18` + ret = +36; the stub gives +4. DEFICIT 32 - exactly the 24-byte SEH frame sub_00011A60 installs plus the 8 bytes of ebx/esi sub_00011AB4 pushes. (b) The 8 inside sub_001E9C10: it is cdecl with one ICALL through an object's vtable+0x60. Recomputed the target from the same globals the ICALL walks - "[T] idx=1 obj=0x01087000 target=0x001E9500" - and measured either side: "[C:ENT] esp=0x00F7FE00" / "[C:RET_A] esp=0x00F7FDF8", with RET_A firing BEFORE `esp += 4`, so the callee popped NEITHER its argument NOR its return address. sub_001E9500 pushes esi then exits at loc_001E9510 to sub_001E9558, and recomp_stubs_unresolved.c:1680 reads `void sub_001E9558(void) { g_esp += 4; /* 0x001E9558: not detected */ }`. Its real epilogue at loc_001E9554 is POP esi + `esp += 8` (ret 4) = +12; the stub gives +4. DEFICIT 8. TOTAL 8 + 32 = 40 = 0x28, matching the measured deficit to the byte, at every level of the chain (#70). NOTE the first slot60 probe printed 0 because it sat at loc_001E9C1E before `ecx` is loaded and read a stale register - the esp readings from that run were still valid and the target was recovered by recomputing the chain from globals instead of trusting a register at a label. THE FIX: seed the real code at 0x001E9558 and 0x00011B2B so both fragments lift properly. This is lifter bug class 3 (generic `g_esp += 4` stubs) from the memory note, and it now has a confirmed instance that costs a boot. NO SWEEP TOOL EXISTS for this class yet and one is clearly worth building - the run reports 8 safe stubs and these two were found only by chasing a specific crash. entries.claim: Seeding sub_00011B2B and sub_001E9558 FIXES the 40-byte leak and the pool corruption with it - kernel_calls 82 -> 330, heap_allocs 22 -> 28, backtrace 4 -> 18 frames through subsystems never entered before. BUT `reached` went DOWN 55 -> 42, so the project's gated signal disagrees with every other measurement. Recording the conflict rather than picking the flattering number
entries.evidence: Applied #71's fix: `seed_missing_functions.py --va 0x00011B2B --apply` (0x00011B2B-0x00011E35, 778 bytes, covering the SEH teardown at loc_00011C3F) and `--va 0x001E9558 --apply` (0x001E9558-0x001E9566, 14 bytes), each followed by replacing its line in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c with a `moved to src/recomp_seed.c` comment or the link fails LNK2005. seed_list.json now records 1162 addresses. MECHANICAL CLAIM VERIFIED DIRECTLY, and this is the part that is not in doubt. After seeding sub_00011B2B alone, re-probed sub_001E8DB0 exactly as before the change: six calls, every one reading IN 0x00F7FE38 / OUT 0x00F7FE24, i.e. IN - OUT = 0x14 where 0x0C was due - 8 bytes short, precisely the sub_001E9558 half still outstanding, and 32 of the 40 already recovered. That is #71's arithmetic (8 + 32) confirmed by measurement, one stub at a time, exactly as the memory note instructs. The reporter also went from 2 calls to 6+, so the boot was already living longer. AFTER BOTH SEEDS, deterministic 2 of 2: kernel_calls 82 -> 330, heap_allocs 22 -> 28, failed_icalls 2 -> 3, safe_stub 8 (unchanged), crash RVA 0xDFC7B3 -> 0xD248B0. THE ORIGINAL CRASH IS GONE: sub_00205170 with esi = 1 off the corrupted pool no longer happens, which is the whole chain #68/#69/#70 predicted. The new backtrace is 18 frames where it was 4, and the outer 10 are code the boot had never executed: sub_0019F22E -> sub_001A1C97 -> sub_0019F196 -> sub_001A1C23 -> sub_00011E40 -> sub_00239E50 -> sub_002282E0 -> sub_00209650 -> sub_00227F50 -> sub_002235D0 -> sub_001F3680 -> sub_001EC720 -> sub_00211530 -> sub_00210E50 -> sub_0020F860 -> sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> sub_001E8F30. esp at the crash is 0x00F7FCCC, a healthy stack address. THE CONFLICT, stated plainly: `reached` (distinct indirect dispatch targets) fell 55 -> 42. Memory says judge on `reached`, and it is pointing the wrong way. The available explanation - and it is an explanation, not a proof - is that `reached` counts vtable DIVERSITY, not depth: the old boot spun inside the allocator's retry machinery repeatedly resolving many distinct vtable slots, and this fix is precisely what stops that retry loop, so fewer distinct indirect targets get touched while far more real work happens. Note also that the kernel_calls cap warning (#33) does NOT apply at 330 - that signal is only distorted when pinned at 4000 - so 82 -> 330 is a genuine 4x. DO NOT let this become a second #30, where a good fix was reverted on a misread signal; equally, do not call it settled. THE HONEST STATUS: the mechanical fix is proven, the predicted corruption is gone, and one signal disagrees. AN INTERMEDIATE READING WAS TAKEN AND IS WORTH KNOWING: after seeding only sub_00011B2B, reached was 43 and esp at the crash was 0xFFFFFF68 - NEGATIVE, an over-pop from the half-fixed state. Seeding the second stub cleared that, which is itself evidence the pair belong together and neither should be left alone. NEXT STEP: settle the `reached` question before building on this. Either find a depth-based progress signal, or instrument distinct-function-entry counts rather than distinct-dispatch-target counts. NEW WALL: read at Xbox VA 0x8B011840 in sub_001E8F30 + 0x180, `fault == esi + 0`, with edi = 2 so the region-walk loop RUNS - note memory records this same function as harmless when MEM32(4) is 0 and the loop is skipped, which is no longer the case. Tree clean: probes stripped, build verified.

entries.claim: `reached` counts ONLY indirect dispatch - RECOMP_ICALL, RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE and RECOMP_ITAIL are the only three callers of recomp_mark_reached(). Direct RECOMP_ABI_CALL sites are plain C calls and are never counted, so `reached` is structurally blind to directly-called code and CAN fall while the boot runs strictly more. Added g_callsite_count to cover the blind spot
entries.evidence: Settled by reading the implementation, not by inference from run numbers. recomp_mark_reached() is defined at recomp_types.h:252 and grep finds exactly THREE call sites, all indirect: RECOMP_ICALL (line ~597), RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE (~634) and RECOMP_ITAIL (~649), each as `if (_fn) { recomp_mark_reached(_va); _fn(); }`. RECOMP_ABI_CALL - the direct-call macro, 1624+ sites in recomp_0015.c alone - expanded to bare `fn()` with no marking at all. So g_reached_count is "distinct INDIRECT targets", never "distinct functions entered". THE HEADER ITSELF ADMITS THIS at recomp_types.h:233: "It counts indirect-call targets, not every function - direct calls are ordinary C calls with nothing to hook. In this engine that is a good proxy: 18,556 generated call sites are indirect, because the whole thing is virtual dispatch through igMetaObject." The proxy argument is sound in general and fails in one specific case: a fix that REMOVES indirect work. That is exactly what #72 did - seeding the two stubs cut a vtable-heavy retry spin out of the allocator, so the boot stopped re-resolving the same slots and ran straight-line code instead. Judged on `reached` alone it read as a regression while kernel_calls went 82 -> 330 and the backtrace 4 -> 18 frames. This retroactively explains #72's conflict and means `reached` should NOT be treated as the sole gate; it is one of two numbers. THE FIX, purely additive and semantically inert: RECOMP_MARK_SITE() in recomp_types.h, one `static uint8_t` per textual call site set on first execution, invoked from BOTH arms of RECOMP_ABI_CALL (the plain one and the RECOMP_CHECK_ABI one). g_callsite_count is defined in recomp_manual.c and printed by recomp_coverage_dump() alongside the existing line. Cost is one predictable branch and one byte of .bss per site; it cannot alter behaviour because it touches no register, no memory model and no control flow. It counts call SITES rather than functions deliberately - finer grained, and marking function entries would mean editing all 30,002 generated bodies instead of one macro. FIRST READING on the current post-seed tree: "distinct=42 of 1032192 dispatch targets reached" and "callsites=177 distinct direct call sites executed", build deterministic at 330/3/28/8. The pre-seed comparison is being measured now by rebuilding recomp_seed.c from a seed list with the two addresses removed (`--from-list ... --apply`, the tool's supported path), with seed_list.json backed up to seed_list.json.bak_settle first. SEPARATE FINDING worth its own work, spotted while reading the header: RECOMP_CHECK_ABI is an EXISTING build mode that validates ebx/esi/edi across every direct call and flags esp leaving the stack range, naming the callee - `recomp_abi_violation()` and `recomp_esp_escape()`. That is an automated detector for the exact bug class (#38, #52, #69, #71) this project has been finding by hand, one probe pair at a time. Nobody appears to have run it. Try a RECOMP_CHECK_ABI build.

entries.claim: The set diff settles #72: the seed fix gained only 4 functions and LOST 17, including sub_001FE670 (the region registrar that fix #44 existed to enable), sub_001ECAD0 (fix #5) and sub_001F83D0/sub_001F8408 (fix #54). It converts silent corruption into an honest allocation failure, so the engine takes give-up branches instead of retry branches. KEEP the seeds - they are provably correct - but the blocker is now #69, why the pool refuses 16 bytes
entries.evidence: MEASURED BY REBUILDING BOTH STATES AND DIFFING THE ADDRESS SETS, not by arguing about scalars. Method: added a [COVERAGE-VA] dump to recomp_coverage_dump() printing every set bit of g_reached as a guest VA; captured the post-seed set; rebuilt the pre-seed tree with `seed_missing_functions.py --from-list <list minus the two addresses> --apply` plus restoring the two stub lines; captured that set; then restored the full 1162-address list and verified the tree returns to 330/3/28/8 exactly. The pre-seed rebuild reproduced 82/2/22/8 exactly, so the two states are faithful. RESULT: before 55, after 42, common 38. ONLY AFTER (4): sub_00194190, sub_002264D0, sub_00227F50, sub_002282E0 - genuinely new ground, and sub_00227F50 and sub_002282E0 both appear in the new 18-frame backtrace. ONLY BEFORE (17): sub_000DDCC0, sub_0013D370, sub_0015FDF0, sub_001E90F0, sub_001ECA40, sub_001ECAD0, sub_001ECAF0, sub_001F0B20, sub_001F14D0, sub_001F1660, sub_001F7020, sub_001F83D0, sub_001F8408, sub_001FA2F0, sub_001FE670, sub_002039A0, sub_0020A8B0. FOURTEEN of the seventeen are in the 0x1E-0x20 allocator/pool/region range, which supports the "stopped thrashing" reading - but THREE OF THEM ARE FUNCTIONS EARLIER FIXES EXISTED TO ENABLE, and that must not be glossed: sub_001FE670 is the region registrar reached only via vtable+0x68 from loc_001F0B03, the exact branch fix #44 repaired (worth reached 37 -> 43); sub_001ECAD0 was fix #5 (54 -> 55); sub_001F83D0 and sub_001F8408 are the jump-table pair from fix #54 (47 -> 54). Those fixes are not wrong and should NOT be reverted, but they are now dormant. INTERPRETATION, and it follows from #69 rather than being invented to fit: the pool genuinely refuses the 16-byte request. Before the seed, the 40-byte leak corrupted edi so `eax + edi` laundered that NULL into the pool's own base address and the null check passed - the engine believed it had succeeded and carried on into its retry/growth machinery. After the seed the null check fires honestly, so the engine takes GIVE-UP branches instead of RETRY branches. That is why the retry machinery went quiet and why kernel_calls still quadrupled: different path, not merely a longer one. VERDICT: keep the seeds. They are mechanically proven (#71/#72), they remove real memory corruption, and reverting would restore a bug. But this is NOT clean forward progress and should not be recorded as such. THE BLOCKER IS NOW #69 - why the pool allocator refuses a 16-byte request - and everything else is downstream of it. ALSO SETTLED, correcting my own prediction: I expected a direct-call counter to show the gain the indirect-only `reached` was missing. It did not. g_callsite_count fell 194 -> 177, agreeing with `reached`. Both coverage counts measure BREADTH, which a retry spin inflates, so neither can distinguish "went further" from "stopped thrashing" - only the set diff can. TOOLING PROMOTED so this is repeatable: tools_data/diff_reached.py plus baseline_reached_preseed.txt and baseline_reached_postseed.txt. Temporary seed lists deleted; seed_list.json back to 1162.

entries.claim: THE POOL REFUSES 16 BYTES BECAUSE OUR OWN KERNEL BRIDGE IGNORES THE REQUESTED BASE ADDRESS. bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory reads base_hint then calls xbox_HeapAlloc(size, 4096) for MEM_RESERVE, returning the bump pointer instead of the requested base. The engine reserves at an address it verified free, gets a different one back, checks `if (returned != requested) fail`, and gives up. Measured off by exactly 0x3000 twice
entries.evidence: Walked the whole chain top to bottom on the CURRENT build (330/3/28/8 deterministic), re-measuring rather than trusting #40/#41 because fix #44 and the #72 seeds both changed the code underneath them. STEP 1 - sub_001F09D0: ten loop iterations, every one ending edi = -1. Probes at all ten labels show CMIT/STAT/UNDO/STA2/WIN/FAIL never fire, so the commit/undo logic #41 analysed is NEVER REACHED on this build. That supersedes #41's picture without contradicting its measurements - the code changed. STEP 2 - the allocator gate: vtable+0x70 is sub_001FE850, whose entire test is `ecx = MEM32(0x46A668) >> 0x1A; edx = MEM32(0x5BBAD0) >> 0x1A; if (ecx <= edx) ok; else return -1`. At identity values MIN=0xFFFFFFFF MAX=0 that is 63 <= 0, false, so it refuses. STEP 3 - the bootstrap: the ONLY writer of MIN and MAX is sub_001FE670's tail (recomp_0015.c:5136-5146, a min/max extender), and its ONLY caller is loc_001F0B03, which is downstream of a SUCCESSFUL allocation. Circular by construction, so something must break the cycle - and that is the fallback at loc_001F09FB. Probed it: "[Q:A4PRE] vtbl=0x003EECB0 target=0x001FFD50" on all 10 calls, "[Q:A4POST] ret=0xFFFFFFFF" on all 10. STEP 4 - walked all 65 labels of sub_001FFDA1, the OS reservation logic (sub_0034D457 queries, sub_0034D3ED reserves/commits, sub_0034D41B releases). The scan WORKS: it walks ebx 0x00000000 -> 0x00010000 -> 0x00780000 -> 0x00F80000 -> 0x0108CA90, testing `mbi.State == 0x10000 (MEM_FREE) && mbi.RegionSize >= edi` at loc_001FFEB0/loc_001FFEBE, and it FINDS a free region of 0x02F70000 - so ledger #35's MEM_FREE work is delivering correctly. It then aligns to base 0x01090000 and reserves 0x140000 bytes with flags 0x2000 (MEM_RESERVE) via sub_0034D3ED at loc_001FFF2D. THE FAILURE, at loc_001FFF3B: eax = 0x0108D000. The call returned a DIFFERENT address than the 0x01090000 requested. loc_001FFF86 loads ecx = the requested base and loc_001FFF8E does `if (eax != ecx) goto loc_0020012B` - the failure exit, which returns MEM32(esp+0x14), seeded to 0xFFFFFFFF by sub_001FFD50. Second attempt identical: requested 0x011D0000, got 0x011CD000. BOTH OFF BY EXACTLY 0x3000. STEP 5 - confirmed in our own source. kernel_bridge.c:388 bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory reads `base_hint = BRIDGE_MEM32(base_ptr)` at line 399 and even LOGS it at 402, handles the MEM_COMMIT-without-RESERVE case at 422, and then at line 435 does `uint32_t xbox_va = xbox_HeapAlloc(size, 4096);` - base_hint is simply DISCARDED for MEM_RESERVE. xbox_memory_layout.c:659 xbox_HeapAlloc is a pure bump allocator with no address parameter at all: `result = (g_heap_next + alignment - 1) & ~(alignment - 1)`. So a reservation at a caller-chosen address is impossible to express. THIS IS A PORT BUG IN OUR KERNEL, NOT A LIFTER BUG AND NOT GAME BEHAVIOUR. The engine is doing the correct and normal thing: query for a free region, reserve exactly there, verify it got what it asked for. PROPOSED FIX: honour base_hint for MEM_RESERVE. Add an xbox_HeapAllocAt(base, size) that, when base >= xbox_HeapHighWater() and base + size <= XBOX_HEAP_BASE + XBOX_HEAP_SIZE, sets g_heap_next = base + size, zero-fills, and returns base exactly. That is consistent with what bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory already reports since #35 - everything from the high-water mark up is MEM_FREE - so any base the engine picks from a MEM_FREE report is by construction above the bump pointer and safe to hand over. Both observed requests (0x01090000 vs bump 0x0108D000, and 0x011D0000 vs 0x011CD000) are ABOVE the bump pointer, so the simple forward-skip covers the measured cases. Fall back to the current behaviour when base_hint is 0. EXPECT ON FIX: the reservation succeeds, sub_001FFDA1 returns a real address, sub_001F09D0 reaches loc_001F0A96 and then loc_001F0B03, sub_001FE670 registers the region, MIN/MAX get real values, and sub_001FE850 stops refusing - which should also revive sub_001FE670, sub_001ECAD0, sub_001F83D0 and sub_001F8408, the functions #74 recorded as going dormant. Measure with tools_data/diff_reached.py against baseline_reached_postseed.txt, not on counts alone. Tree clean: 233 probe lines stripped.

entries.claim: FIXED #75: bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory now honours base_hint via a new xbox_HeapAllocAt(). The engine gets the exact address it reserves, registers its memory region, and STOPS ENTERING THE OOM REPORTER ENTIRELY. reached 42 -> 63 and callsites 177 -> 248, beating the all-time best of 55 with 20 functions that never ran in ANY previous state. Best result of 2026-08-07
entries.evidence: THE FIX, entirely in our kernel, no lifter or generated code touched. Added xbox_HeapAllocAt(base, size) in xbox_memory_layout.c: refuses when base < g_heap_next (that would overlap a live allocation and would mean our MEM_FREE reporting disagrees with the allocator - worth seeing, not papering over) or when base+size runs past the heap end; otherwise sets g_heap_next = base + size, zero-fills, and returns base EXACTLY. Declared in xbox_memory_layout.h. kernel_bridge.c:435 changed from `xbox_HeapAlloc(size, 4096)` to `base_hint ? xbox_HeapAllocAt(base_hint, size) : xbox_HeapAlloc(size, 4096)`. Safe by construction: since #35 the bridge reports everything from xbox_HeapHighWater() up as MEM_FREE, so a base the engine chose from our own report is at or above the bump pointer. IT WORKS, first try, deterministic 2 of 2: "[HEAP] #14: AT 0x01090000 size=1310720 -> 0x01090000..0x011D0000 (used 2424832/50855936)" - the engine asked for 0x01090000 and got 0x01090000, where before it got 0x0108D000 and gave up. SIGNALS: reached 42 -> 63, callsites 177 -> 248. 63 BEATS THE ALL-TIME BEST OF 55. kernel_calls fell 330 -> 44 and heap_allocs 28 -> 20, which is EXPECTED and good - the 330 was dominated by the failing NtQueryVirtualMemory scan loop hammering the address space, and that loop is gone because the first reservation now succeeds. This is the case #73/#74 warned about, in reverse: judge on the SET, not the count. SET DIFF vs the pre-fix state (tools_data/diff_reached.py): 27 gained, 6 lost. The six lost are precisely the failure path and are CORRECT to lose - sub_00011A60 (the fatal out-of-memory reporter itself), sub_001E8DB0 (the vtable+0x54 thunk that reaches it), sub_001E9500 (whose sub_001E9558 stub was seeded in #72), plus sub_00194190, sub_00227F50, sub_002282E0. THE BOOT NO LONGER ENTERS THE OOM REPORTER AT ALL. sub_001FE670, the region registrar, is BACK - confirming #75's prediction and closing the circular dependency: reservation succeeds -> loc_001F0B03 runs -> MIN/MAX at 0x46A668/0x5BBAD0 get real values -> sub_001FE850's gate stops refusing. SET DIFF vs the ORIGINAL 55-function best: 63 reached, 43 common, and 20 functions that never ran in ANY previous state, mostly a whole band of new subsystems - sub_002181F0, sub_00219A10, sub_0021A170, sub_0021C680, sub_0021DB50, sub_0021E190, sub_0021F190, sub_00220040, sub_00221F50, sub_002221E0, sub_00226250. PREDICTION PARTLY WRONG, recorded honestly: #75 predicted all four dormant functions would revive. Only sub_001FE670 did. sub_001ECAD0, sub_001F83D0 and sub_001F8408 are still NOT reached, so whatever gated them is a separate matter and should not be assumed fixed. NEW WALL: read at Xbox VA 0x74C98508 in sub_00221F50 + 0x187 (recomp_0016.c ~17670), reached through 12 frames: sub_001A1C97 -> sub_0019F22E -> sub_0019F196 -> sub_001A1C23 -> sub_00011E40 -> sub_00239E50 -> sub_0023666F -> sub_002366BC -> sub_00209650 -> sub_002221E0 -> sub_002235D0 -> sub_00221F50. Every register at the crash is a pointer INSIDE the newly reserved region (eax=0x01091AB1, ecx=0x01091B50, edi=0x01091AB0, esi=0x01091B18, all within 0x01090000..0x011D0000), so the engine is genuinely USING the memory it reserved. esp=0x00F7FDE4 is healthy. ALSO WORTH SEEDING: one of the 3 failed indirect calls is target 0x00221E50, a plausible code address rather than garbage - a genuinely missing function. Tree clean, no probes.

entries.claim: Seeding the single missing 153-byte function sub_00221E50 took reached 63 -> 99 and callsites 248 -> 382 with 36 functions gained and ZERO lost - the first unambiguous "strictly more code ran" result on this project. A failed-icall target that disassembles cleanly is the cheapest lead available and should be checked at EVERY wall
entries.evidence: Method that found it, and it was almost free: triage prints "failed indirect calls this run" with their targets. After #76 those were 0x00000001, 0x00000000 and 0x00221E50. The first two are garbage pointers; the third is a plausible code address AND sits immediately below the crashing function sub_00221F50 in the same subsystem. `search sub_00221E50` returned ZERO hits - not defined, not even stubbed in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c - so the ICALL had nothing to resolve to and fell through to recomp_icall_fail_log. `seed_missing_functions.py --va 0x00221E50` disassembled a clean extent 0x00221E50-0x00221EE9 (153 bytes), which is the confirmation the notes call for: a clean disassembly means a genuinely missing function, nonsense means a bad pointer. Seeded with --apply (seed_list.json now 1163). NO STUB LINE TO REMOVE, unlike #72 - the function was absent entirely rather than stubbed, so there was no LNK2005 risk. RESULT, deterministic 2 of 2: reached 63 -> 99, callsites 248 -> 382, heap_allocs 20 -> 25, kernel_calls unchanged at 44, failed_icalls unchanged at 3. SET DIFF vs baseline_reached_best63.txt: 36 gained, 0 LOST. diff_reached.py's verdict line reads "strictly more code ran. Unambiguous progress." That is the first time this project has produced a clean gain with no losses - #72 was 4 gained / 17 lost and #76 was 27 gained / 6 lost, both needing interpretation. This one needs none. THE 36: sub_0021B7D0, sub_0021EED0, sub_0021EFB0, sub_00220870, sub_00221E50, sub_00226550, sub_00226700, sub_00227CC0, sub_00227E00, sub_00227F50, sub_002282E0, sub_002287E0, sub_002289E0, sub_00229260, sub_00229360, sub_002293E0, sub_00229960, sub_00229F80, sub_0022A0B0, sub_0022A3C0, sub_0022AC70, sub_0022B850, sub_0022B9E0, sub_0022DFC0, sub_0022E0C0, sub_0022E3C0, sub_0022F420, sub_0022F4F0, sub_00230880, sub_002316D0, sub_00231820, sub_00233490, sub_00235FE0, sub_002361A0, sub_00236280, sub_002362C0 - an entire band of 0x0022xxxx/0x0023xxxx the boot had never entered. One 153-byte function was gating all of it. GENERAL LESSON worth applying at every future wall: check triage's failed-icall targets FIRST. It costs one search and one dry-run, and the payoff here was larger than any lifter repair made today. NEW WALL: read at Xbox VA 0xFFFFFFFF in sub_0022C2A0 + 0x279 (recomp_0016.c ~40112), fault == ecx + 0 with ecx = -1, eax/edi/esi all NULL. Backtrace sub_001A1C97 -> sub_0019F22E -> sub_0019F196 -> sub_001A1C23 -> sub_00011E40 -> sub_00239E50 -> sub_002392E0 -> sub_0022C2A0. WATCH THIS: esp = 0x00F80120, which is ABOVE XBOX_HEAP_BASE 0x00F80000 and therefore PAST THE TOP OF THE STACK (the stack region is 0x00780000-0x00F80000, growing down). That is a stack UNDERFLOW - too many pops - not the overflow direction. triage labels it "heap" because the address is in the heap range, which is misleading here. Investigate whether the newly seeded fragments over-pop before trusting the next measurement. AND THE SAME LEAD IS AVAILABLE AGAIN: this run's failed icalls are 0x00000001, 0x00000000 and 0x00216F70; sub_00216F70 does not exist and dry-runs to a clean 6-byte extent 0x00216F70-0x00216F76, a thunk or trivial getter. Seeding it now.
