So the leak is closed and sub_0020F209 merely being ON the backtrace proves nothing about it. THIS IS THE EXACT TRAP THIS PROJECT KEEPS RECORDING - "a refutation expires when the code under it changes", and equally an INSTRUCTION expires. #40 said do not fix the leak, #70 retracted that and said fix it, #71/#72 then fixed it, and I quoted #70 as if it were current. Read the LATEST entry on a function, not the first one that matches.

[2] THE SHIFT IDIOM IS CORRECTLY LIFTED - checked because it looked wrong. The crash site walks a free list with a tagged-pointer trick:
    edx = MEM32(ebx + 0x48);
    edx = edx >> 0x1F;   edx = edx << 3;   edx = edx | 4;
    ebp = MEM32(edx + ebx);
On a uint32_t, `>> 0x1F` is logical and yields 0 or 1, so the offset is +4 or +0xC. Had the original been `sar`, the value would be 0 or -1 and the offsets +4 or -4, which would be a serious mis-lift. Raw bytes at 0x002052FB settle it:
    8B 53 48        mov edx, [ebx+0x48]
    83 C3 48        add ebx, 0x48
    C1 EA 1F        shr edx, 0x1F        <- /5 = SHR, logical. Not sar.
    C1 E2 03        shl edx, 3
    83 CA 04        or  edx, 4
    8B 2C 1A        mov ebp, [edx+ebx]
    8D 04 1A        lea eax, [edx+ebx]
    89 30           mov [eax], esi
So the lift matches the original instruction-for-instruction and there is no defect at this site. Do not "fix" it.

WHAT THE CRASH ACTUALLY IS, still open: sub_00205170+0x7D1 faults reading MEM32(edx) with edx = 0x830C048B, a value whose top bit is set - i.e. a TAGGED word being used as a raw address. Registers: eax=0x0109DF60 (heap), esi=0x010983F5 (heap but NOT 4-byte aligned, which is itself suspicious for an object pointer), ebx=4, edi=0x5B6B, ecx=0x003F1160 (.rdata). This is the real allocator's free list, exercised for the first time now that 826 allocations happen instead of 92. NEXT: find where 0x830C048B enters the list, and why esi is misaligned - probe the free-list writers rather than the reader, since the reader is now proven faithful.

entries.claim: THE POST-#136 CRASH IS PINNED, and it is a DATA defect, not a lifter one. sub_00205170's backward-coalesce at loc_00205276 reads the previous block's boundary tag at MEM32(esi-4) and gets 0x00001003 - a size of 0x1000 with the low flag bits 3 still set. The original x86 does `mov ecx,[esi-4]; sub esi,ecx` with NO masking instruction (verified opcode-for-opcode), so it expects a CLEAN size there. Subtracting the flagged word gives esi = 0x010993F8 - 0x1003 = 0x010983F5, misaligned by 3 and exactly the crash register, after which every free-list link read out of that bogus block is garbage - which is where 0x830C048B comes from. Reading a flagged value where a clean footer belongs is the signature of a HEADER being read where a FOOTER should be. It happens exactly ONCE in the boot.
entries.evidence:
METHOD: two probe builds, both stripped. Tree clean and probe-free, rebuilt, deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 4000 (cap) / failed_icalls 274 / heap_allocs 826 / safe_stub 8, crash unchanged at RVA 0xEAD9A1 = sub_00205170 + 0x7D1.

[1] A WRONG FIRST GUESS, recorded so it is not repeated. I first placed the probe at loc_002052CB, having matched triage's "fault == edx + 0x0" to the bare `ecx = MEM32(edx)` in that block. It fired ZERO times - that block never executes. The live path takes the other arm of the branch at loc_002052BA. Attribution by reading source and matching a register expression is a guess; the probe is what settles it.

[2] ALSO CORRECTED: I briefly decoded guest bytes at guest VA 0x00205941 because triage reported "sub_00205170 + 0x7D1". That offset is into the NATIVE x64 build, not guest space, so the decode was meaningless. Resolving the crash RVA properly against the map's Rva+Base column (0xEAD9A1 - 0xEAD1D0 = 0x7D1, sub_00205170 at 0000000140ead1d0) confirms triage's attribution was right all along; only my use of the offset was wrong. Guest offsets and native offsets are not interchangeable.

[3] THE MEASUREMENT. Probe at loc_00205276 printing esi, the boundary tag, and the resulting pointer. It fires exactly ONCE in the entire boot:
  [PCOA] esi=010993F8 foot=00001003 newesi=010983F5
0x010993F8 - 0x00001003 = 0x010983F5, which is the crash dump's esi exactly, and is misaligned by 3.

[4] THE LIFT IS FAITHFUL - checked before blaming it. Raw bytes at 0x00205276:
    8B 4E FC    mov ecx, [esi-4]
    2B F1       sub esi, ecx
    03 F9       add edi, ecx
    8B 0E       mov ecx, [esi]
    C1 E9 1F    shr ecx, 0x1F
    C1 E1 03    shl ecx, 3
    83 C9 04    or  ecx, 4
There is NO and/mask instruction between the load and the subtract. The original genuinely expects MEM32(esi-4) to hold a clean size. Our lifted C matches instruction-for-instruction. Do not "fix" this site by adding a mask - that would be scaffolding over corrupt data and would silently paper over the real defect.

[5] WHAT THE VALUE MEANS. 0x1003 is 0x1000 with the low three bits set. In a boundary-tag allocator the HEADER carries size|flags and the FOOTER carries the clean size, so reading 0x1003 at [esi-4] means the word being read is a header, or a footer that was never written, or the block boundary is off by the header size. The whole downstream mess follows mechanically: bogus block -> bogus tag -> bogus links -> MEM32(0x830C048B) faults.

[6] WHY IT ONLY SURFACED NOW. This is the first boot in which the real allocator is exercised at scale - heap_allocs went 92 -> 826 with #136 - so the backward coalesce runs for the first time. The defect was always latent.

NEXT: find who writes the boundary tag at 0x010993F4 (= esi-4). Either a free/split path is writing size|flags where a clean size belongs, or the previous block never wrote a footer at all and the read is landing on a header. Probe the writers of that word rather than the reader - the reader is now proven faithful. Note also that the 184/217 kernel-ordinal recursion pinned at the 4000 cap is still unexplained and may or may not be related; ordinal 217 is NtQueryVirtualMemory, which ledgers #33/#35 have history with.

entries.claim: THE DEFECT IS UPSTREAM OF THE ALLOCATOR: sub_00205170's free path runs exactly three times, and the fatal third call is handed a "block" whose header word is a HEAP POINTER (0x01096C60) rather than a packed size|flags. The two healthy calls show real headers, 0x00000203 and 0x00000403, both with bit 0 (PREV_IN_USE) SET so the backward coalesce is correctly skipped. The bad block's pointer-header has bit 0 clear, so the coalesce fires and reads user data as a boundary tag. So #138's "footer has flag bits set" is a SYMPTOM - 0x1003 is not a corrupted footer at all, it is whatever happened to sit at that address, read as one because a non-block was freed.
entries.evidence:
METHOD: one probe at loc_002051F1 (the free path's entry decode) printing the block, its header word and the word at block-4. Probe stripped, rebuilt, deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 4000 (cap) / failed_icalls 274 / heap_allocs 826 / safe_stub 8, crash unchanged at RVA 0xEAD9A1.

[1] ALL THREE CALLS, and that is the whole set:
  [PHDR] blk=01090004 hdr=00000203 foot=00000000
  [PHDR] blk=01096DC4 hdr=00000403 foot=00000000
  [PHDR] blk=010993F8 hdr=01096C60 foot=00001003
The first two are healthy. Their headers are small packed words - the size lives in bits 5.. and the low bits are flags - and both have bit 0 SET, i.e. PREV_IN_USE, so the gate at loc_00205264 (`test bl,1; jne`) correctly skips the backward coalesce and neither reads a footer.

[2] THE THIRD IS NOT A BLOCK. Its header word reads 0x01096C60, which is a heap POINTER, not a packed header. Bit 0 of a pointer to a 32-bit-aligned object is 0, so the PREV_IN_USE gate reads "previous block is free" and the coalesce runs. MEM32(esi-4) then returns 0x00001003, which is simply whatever occupies that address - not a boundary tag at all.

[3] SO #138's FRAMING NEEDS CORRECTING. #138 said the boundary tag "has flag bits set" and asked who writes size|flags into a footer slot. That question is malformed: nothing wrote a bad footer. The read is bogus because the object being freed is not a heap block, so there is no footer there to write. Chasing footer writers would have been chasing a value that was never a footer. #138's other conclusions stand - the reader is faithful, the lift is correct, and no mask should be added.

[4] WHERE 0x01096C60 POINTS. It is in the same neighbourhood as the type-system member descriptors this session has been tracing (0x01096B88 the metaclass container, 0x01096D20, 0x01096FA0, 0x01096FD8 the +0x28 member). So the word at 0x010993F8 looks like a link or element-array pointer belonging to a live type-system object, which means 0x010993F8 is an object interior or an object that was never allocated by this allocator - and it is being handed to free.

[5] WHY IT ONLY APPEARS NOW: the free path runs three times in this boot and only since #136, which took heap_allocs from 92 to 826 and put the real allocator in service. The two healthy frees prove the allocator itself is working correctly.

NEXT: find the CALLER that frees 0x010993F8. The backtrace of #136 shows the chain reaching sub_00205170 via sub_0020A8B0 <- sub_001E8F30 <- sub_0020F209, but that is the crashing frame, not necessarily the caller of free. Probe sub_00205170's entry for the incoming pointer and correlate with the free_object_instance / refcount-drop paths (FUN_0020e960's tail does a refcount decrement and calls free_object_instance when it hits zero, and sub_002041D0 appears in the same family). The likely shapes are: a refcount reaching zero on an object that was never heap-allocated, or a pointer being freed at the wrong offset (interior rather than block start). Do NOT patch sub_00205170 - it is behaving correctly given what it is handed.

entries.claim: CORRECTS #139's NEXT STEP: sub_00205170 is not a free(ptr) function. Its argument is the ALLOCATOR (`this`), and it walks a DEFERRED-FREE ARRAY held inside the pool at this+0x70 - entry count from MEM32(pool) >> 3, entries running from pool+4. So the three blocks #139 measured are entries ALREADY QUEUED in that array, not pointers handed to a free call. "Find the caller that frees 0x010993F8" is therefore the wrong question - no caller does. The right question is what ENQUEUED 0x010993F8 into the deferred-free array.
entries.evidence:
No code changed, no build needed; tree is still at #136's state, deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 4000 (cap) / failed_icalls 274 / heap_allocs 826 / safe_stub 8.

[1] GHIDRA XREFS show every caller passing the allocator, not a block. Eight call sites, and the shape is identical at all of them - e.g. FUN_0020a8b0: `iVar6 = *(int *)((int)this + 0x70); FUN_00205170(this);`, and FUN_0020f860 calls `FUN_00205170(this)` three times. FUN_002056d0 calls it as `FUN_00205170(param_1)` guarded on `param_1[0x28] == 0 && param_1[0x29] == 0`.

[2] THE LIFTED ENTRY CONFIRMS THE SHAPE:
    edi = ecx;                       /* this = the allocator */
    if (MEM32(edi + 0xB8) >= 3) ...  /* two icalls on vtable+0x1A8 */
  loc_002051A1:
    ecx = MEM32(edi + 0x70);         /* THE POOL */
    eax = MEM32(ecx);
    if (eax == 0) return;            /* nothing queued */
    eax = eax & 0xFFFFFFFD;          /* clear a flag bit */
    MEM32(ecx) = eax;
    eax = eax >> 3;                  /* ENTRY COUNT */
    edx = ecx + eax * 4 + -4;        /* end of array */
    eax = ecx + 4;                   /* start of array */
So it is a deferred-free / consolidation pass over an array of queued pointers, which also matches ledger #114's description of it walking a "deferred-free array" at this+0x70.

[3] WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE. #139's measurement stands exactly as recorded - three entries processed, two with healthy packed headers (0x203 and 0x403, PREV_IN_USE set) and one, 0x010993F8, whose first word is the heap pointer 0x01096C60 so the coalesce fires on a non-block. There is no such caller; the pointer is already sitting in the array by the time sub_00205170 runs.

[4] THE CORRECTED QUESTION: what writes 0x010993F8 into the deferred-free array? Per #133 the live pool is 0x01089A90, so the array begins at 0x01089A94 and the enqueue path is whatever appends to it and bumps the count word at MEM32(pool). Instrument the ENQUEUE, not any free() caller. A one-shot watch is not enough here (it disarms on the first write and #127/#136 both show system-DLL RIPs prove nothing about origin), so use probes on the enqueue site once located.

[5] METHOD NOTE, third instance this session. #128 was reading a prior entry's displayed evidence as its full evidence; #131 was a probe placed after an icall reporting the previous iteration; this one is inferring a function's role from its name-shaped behaviour instead of reading its signature. In all three the measurement was right and the INTERPRETATION was wrong. Read what the function is actually given before naming what it does.

entries.claim: NOTHING ENQUEUED 0x010993F8 - THERE IS NO QUEUE. On the fatal third call, sub_00205170 is invoked on an allocator whose pool at +0x70 is NULL, so MEM32(0) is read as the entry-count word (0x03FEE024, giving a huge count) and the "array entries" come straight out of MAPPED GUEST PAGE 0 - 0x010993F8 is simply the word at guest address 4. This is the project's recurring page-0 pattern: a NULL pointer plus a mapped page 0 fabricates a plausible-looking array. It also corrects #140's corrected question, and means a POOL-LESS allocator is still reaching this code path after #136.

[1] ALL THREE CALLS, and the third is the whole story:
  [PQ] pool=01089A90 cnt=0000004B e0=00000000 e1=01090004 e2=00000000 e3=00000000
  [PQ] pool=01089A90 cnt=0000004B e0=00000000 e1=00000000 e2=00000000 e3=01096DC4
  [PQ] pool=00000000 cnt=03FEE024 e0=00000000 e1=010993F8 e2=0000001A e3=00000006
The first two run on the GOOD pool 0x01089A90 with a sane count (0x4B >> 3 = 9 entries) and process real blocks - which is why #139 saw healthy packed headers for them. The third runs with pool = 0x00000000.

[2] WHAT A NULL POOL PRODUCES HERE. The function does `ecx = MEM32(edi + 0x70); eax = MEM32(ecx); ... eax >>= 3; edx = ecx + eax*4 - 4; eax = ecx + 4`. With ecx = 0 that is MEM32(0) for the count - measured 0x03FEE024, i.e. 0x7FDC04 entries - and the array base becomes guest address 4. So every "entry" is a page-0 word. 0x010993F8 is MEM32(4). It was never enqueued by anybody.

[3] SO #140's CORRECTED QUESTION IS ALSO WRONG, and I am recording that explicitly. #139 asked for the caller that frees the pointer; #140 corrected that to "what enqueued it into the deferred-free array". Neither exists. #140's structural reading of the function is still right - it does walk a deferred-free array at this+0x70 - but on the fatal call there is no array at all. Both questions were built on the assumption that the data structure was real, and the probe shows the pointer to it is NULL.

[4] WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG: a pool-less allocator reaches sub_00205170. #133 measured all twelve prototypes at +0x70 = NULL while the working allocator 0x01088A90 has +0x70 = 0x01089A90. Two of the three calls here use the good pool, so #136's ownership fix did take effect for those; the third still arrives with a pool-less object as `this`. Note also that the original x86 has NO null check on +0x70 - it cannot, because in the real game the pool is always present - so this is not a missing guard, it is a wrong `this`.

[5] METHOD NOTE, and this is the fourth interpretation error in a row this session (#128, #131, #140, and now #140's replacement question). The pattern is identical every time: the MEASUREMENT was sound and the STORY I built around it was not. Here I twice asked "who put this pointer there" without first checking whether the container holding it was real. CHECK THAT A POINTER IS NON-NULL BEFORE REASONING ABOUT WHAT IT POINTS TO - especially on this project, where guest page 0 is mapped and makes every NULL deref return plausible data instead of faulting.

NEXT: identify WHICH allocator object is passed as `this` on that third call and who calls it. Probe sub_00205170's entry printing ecx (this), MEM32(ecx + 0x70) and MEM32(ecx) (its vtable), and correlate against the twelve at 0x0120D000..0x01218000 and the good 0x01088A90. Then find that call site among the eight Ghidra lists - FUN_0020a8b0, FUN_0020f860 (three sites), FUN_0020aa90 (two sites), FUN_002056d0, FUN_0011e4a0. entries.claim: SECOND REAL FIX THIS SESSION, found by chasing an exact esi/edi SWAP: sub_00209EC0 tail-jumps to sub_00209F19 when ecx == 0, and sub_00209F19 DID NOT EXIST - recomp_stubs_unresolved.c:1810 held the generic `void sub_00209F19(void) { g_esp += 4; }`. The real 12-byte fragment is `mov eax,[esi+8]; mov [ebx+eax],edi; pop edi; pop esi; pop ebx; ret 8`, so the stub skipped BOTH the store that publishes the new sub-object AND all three register pops. Measured directly before the fix: across the sub_00209EC0 call, esi went 01096DC8 -> 01096FD8 and edi went 01096FD8 -> 01096DC8, an exact swap, after which the caller decremented the MEMBER descriptor's refcount to zero and freed it instead of the container. Textbook class-2b, fourth confirmed instance after #46, #71 and #122.

[2] RULED OUT sub_002096B0. It uses the same `this - desc[0x20]` idiom, so it was the obvious suspect. A probe at its call site caught all 33 calls and every one is clean: off=00000000 and q=this, e.g. this=01098CC0 desc=01097728 off=0 q=01098CC0. Not the source.

[3] THE SOURCE, at sub_002041D0 line 16950 `esi = esi - MEM32(eax + 0x20)` immediately before the sub_001E8E20 call. One probe, one hit, and it accounts for every bit of the fatal value:
  [PQ41D0] 041D0 obj=00000001 desc=00000000 off=0A000000 q=F6000001

entries.claim: THIRD FIX THIS SESSION, and it is the documented `_icall_esp` class caught live rather than latent. sub_001EA770 captured `_icall_esp = g_esp` BEFORE its four callee-save pushes, so when its vtable+0x50 ICALL failed, RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE rolled g_esp back PAST the saved ebx/ebp/esi/edi and the epilogue's four POPs read the wrong slots. Measured: sub_002041D0's esi is 0x17 at loc_00204229 and 0x00000001 at loc_00204230, and sub_001EA770 is the only call between them. Fix is to capture _icall_esp after the register saves, immediately before the call. entries.evidence:
METHOD: a four-point then six-point bisect inside sub_002041D0, then the one-line fix, then build + 2 runs + diff_reached. Probes stripped, rebuilt, deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 226 / failed_icalls 272 / heap_allocs 95 / safe_stub 8. manual_edits extract/verify 1066/1066, so the fix survives regeneration.

[1] FIRST, #143's OPEN DISCREPANCY IS RESOLVED. #143 could not reconcile an entry probe showing ecx=4 and ecx=0x17 against a later probe showing esi=1, and honestly recorded it as unresolved. Running both points in ONE build settles it: [PA1] ENTRY this=00000004, [PA1] ENTRY this=00000017, [PA2] SUBTRACT esi=00000001 desc=00000000. Two calls total, and on the second one esi CHANGES between entry and the subtraction. So esi was being clobbered inside the function - neither probe was wrong.

[2] THE BISECT, six probes in one run:
  [PC3] at421B esi=00000017   (before the vtable+0x28 icall)
  [PC5] at4222 esi=00000017   (after it, before sub_001EA730)
  [PC6] at4229 esi=00000017   (after sub_001EA730, before sub_001EA770)
  [PC4] at4230 esi=00000001   (after sub_001EA770)
sub_001EA770 is the only call between the last two points. Note the lifted sub_002041D0 assigns esi exactly once, at `esi = ecx` on entry, so nothing in its own body could have changed it - the clobber had to come from a callee.

[3] THE DEFECT in sub_001EA770 (recomp_0014.c). Its prologue pushes ebx, ebp, esi, edi and its epilogue pops edi, esi, ebp, ebx - correctly reversed, so the function looks innocent. But the generated code opened the block with `uint32_t _icall_esp = g_esp;` BEFORE those four pushes and then used it for the vtable+0x50 ICALL. RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE restores g_esp = _icall_esp on failure, which discards the four saved registers.

[4] AND THE ICALL DOES FAIL HERE. sub_002041D0 calls it with this = 0x17, so `eax = MEM32(edi)` reads MEM32(0x17) out of mapped guest page 0, the "vtable" is junk, and MEM32(junk + 0x50) is not a real target. The #144 census independently lists sub_001EA770 with 8 page-0 sites including reads of guest 0x17 and 0x50 - exactly this path.

[5] FIX: move `uint32_t _icall_esp = g_esp;` to sit after the four PUSH32 lines and immediately before the ICALL, with a comment recording the original instruction order (push ebx/ebp/esi/edi; mov edi,ecx; mov eax,[edi]; call [eax+0x50] - no arguments pushed, so the correct restore point is right before the call).

[6] MEASURED. Deterministic 2 of 2 before and after. reached 158 -> 158, callsites unchanged, kernel_calls/failed_icalls/heap_allocs/safe_stub all unchanged at 226/272/95/8. diff_reached: "identical sets - the change moved no coverage at all." BUT IT IS EXERCISED, which is the important distinction from ledger #119: the crash's fault address moves from 0xF5FFFFFD to 0xF6010013. That is esi arriving at the subtraction as 0x17 (its correct value) instead of the corrupted 1, so the query becomes 0x17 - <page-0 word> rather than 1 - <page-0 word>. Behaviour changed; coverage did not.

[7] KEPT, on the #72/#78/#89 precedent - provably correct against the original instruction order, and demonstrably exercised. It does not move the wall because the wall is not this bug: sub_002041D0 is still being called with a small integer as `this`, and that remains the open root cause.

[8] THIS IS TASK B2's CLASS, and it closes only ONE site. DEBUGGING_NOTES.md records the same defect at sub_00209650 and notes 15 further esp-relative ICALL sites of similar shape that were deliberately left unswept because each needs per-site disassembly. #130 flagged this exact pattern in sub_001EA600 as a latent hazard; here it was live. The generator-level fix is translator.py's _fixup_icall_esp_save, which walks backwards over consecutive PUSH32 lines and cannot tell an argument push from a callee-saved register save - that remains unfixed and is the real remedy.

NEXT, unchanged: find what calls sub_002041D0 with this = 4 and this = 0x17. Those are the only two calls in the boot and both are small integers, so the caller is passing something that is not an object pointer at all.

entries.claim: THE CALLER SEARCH NARROWED, and two candidate paths are RULED OUT. sub_002041D0 is called exactly twice in the boot, with this = 0x00000004 and this = 0x00000017, and both calls carry an identical icall context: the last three targets are sub_001EC770 (vtable+0x144, the block-size query), sub_001FBA90 (vtable+0x148, the ownership predicate) and sub_001EC220.   [PTR41] free this=00000017 t1=001EC770 t2=001FBA90 t3=001EC220 t4=001FBA90 t5=001EC220

Ghidra confirms sub_001EC770 reads a block header at param_1-4 and decodes a packed size, so on a small integer it is reading page 0.

[6] WHAT THIS MEANS. The two frees are not a caller passing a loop index by mistake in one place - they are the allocator's own bookkeeping path operating on values that are not pointers, with the ownership and size queries happening first. That points at whatever produced those values as object pointers, upstream of the query pair, rather than at a single bad call site.

NEXT: instrument sub_001EC220 (t3, the third target in both traces and not yet examined) and the caller of the query pair, to find where 4 and 0x17 are first treated as objects. entries.claim: CORRECTS #146: the allocator query pair is NOT being run on the small integers. #146 concluded that the vtable+0x144 size query and vtable+0x148 ownership predicate preceding each bad free were operating on 4 and 0x17. Measured: the size query sub_001EC770 fires 351 times in the boot, ALWAYS with the good allocator 0x01088A90 and always with healthy pointers (0x01098D70, 0x01090258, ...), and NEVER with 4 or 0x17. The g_icall_trace ring buffer records temporal adjacency of icall TARGETS, not argument identity - so those queries are ambient allocator traffic that merely happens to precede the free, not a causal chain into it. Also identified: sub_001EC220 is vtable+0x78, a one-line getter returning MEM8(this + 0x74), i.e. the "is this allocator eligible" check in sub_001E8E20's walk - so the t3/t2 pattern in the trace is just that walk, not a free preamble.
entries.evidence:
METHOD: one probe at sub_001EC770's entry printing the allocator and the pointer argument. Stripped afterwards; rebuilt and verified deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 226 / failed_icalls 272 / heap_allocs 95 / safe_stub 8, crash unchanged at sub_001FBA90+0x76, tree probe-free, manual_edits 1066/1066.

[1] THE MEASUREMENT. [PSZ] fires 351 times. Every single call has allocr=01088A90 - the working allocator - and a healthy heap pointer, the tail being ptr=01098D70 five times then ptr=01090258. Not one call carries 4 or 0x17.

[2] SO #146's READING WAS WRONG in one specific and important way. Its facts stand: sub_002041D0 is called exactly twice, with this=4 and this=0x17, and both calls are immediately preceded in g_icall_trace by targets 001EC770, 001FBA90 and 001EC220. What does NOT follow, and what #146 asserted, is that those queries were being performed ON the small integers. They were not. I read temporal adjacency in a ring buffer as argument identity.

[3] WHAT THE TRACE ACTUALLY SHOWS. sub_001EC220 is vtable+0x78 (DATA reference from 0x003f47e8), a one-instruction getter returning MEM8(this + 0x74). sub_001FBA90 is vtable+0x148. Those two together are exactly sub_001E8E20's ownership walk - "is this candidate eligible, does it own the pointer" - repeated per candidate, and sub_001EC770 is vtable+0x144, a size query. So the trace is ordinary allocator traffic on real pointers that happens to be the last thing logged before the free. The ring buffer holds 16 entries and no caller identity at all.

[4] THE STANDING LIMIT ON THIS INSTRUMENT, worth recording since it has now helped once and misled once. g_icall_trace gave the real answer in #134 because there the question was "what dispatched this function", and the function itself appeared in the trace. It misleads when the question is "who called this function with this argument", because it records neither callers nor arguments. Use it to identify a dispatch, never to attribute an argument.

[5] STILL TRUE AND STILL THE OPEN QUESTION: sub_002041D0 is called exactly twice in the whole boot and both times with a small integer as `this`. #146's eliminations also stand on their own measurements - sub_002235D0's free site carries healthy pointers on all 11 of its calls, and sub_0020E5A0 preserves esi across all 11.

entries.claim: THE CALLER IS FOUND, and it is sub_002235D0's free site at loc_00223758 - which #146 WRONGLY ELIMINATED. Captured directly with MSVC's _ReturnAddress() at sub_002041D0's entry: both bad frees return to 0x00007FF68F3C33D1, which resolves through build/xmen_legends_recomp.map to sub_002235D0 + 0xE01 - exactly what #142's triage backtrace said. entries.evidence:
METHOD: three probe builds. All stripped; rebuilt and verified deterministic 2 of 2 at kernel_calls 226 / failed_icalls 272 / heap_allocs 95 / safe_stub 8, crash unchanged at sub_001FBA90+0x76, tree probe-free, manual_edits 1066/1066.

[1] THE INSTRUMENT THAT FINALLY WORKED, and it is worth adding to the toolkit. Every lifted guest function is a real native C function, so MSVC's `_ReturnAddress()` intrinsic at a function's entry yields the NATIVE caller address. It compiles inside a probe with no extra include. Both bad frees give ret=0x00007FF68F3C33D1. Resolving it: the crash line gives RIP=0x7FF68FBDB9F6 with RVA=0x179B9F6, so the image base for that run is 0x7FF68E440000 and the return RVA is 0xF833D1; against the map's Rva+Base column that lands inside sub_002235D0 (0000000140f825d0), at +0xE01. [2] IT CONFIRMS THE BACKTRACE AND REFUTES MY OWN #146. #142's triage listed sub_002235D0 + 0xE01 directly beneath sub_002041D0. That was correct. #146 declared it eliminated.

[3] WHY #146 GOT IT WRONG, and the cause is embarrassing and worth recording plainly. I probed loc_00223738/loc_00223748, got 11 results, and displayed them with `head -10` over an interleaved two-probe grep - so I saw only the first five pairs, all healthy, and concluded the site was innocent.   esi=00000004 rc=00000000      <- entry 7
  esi=01098260 rc=1 / 01098728 rc=1 / 01098A68 rc=1
  esi=00000017 rc=00000000      <- entry 11
and a probe at the free call itself, loc_00223758, fires EXACTLY TWICE: esi=00000004 and esi=00000017.

[4] THIS IS THE THIRD TIME THIS SESSION THE SAME MISTAKE HAS COST AN ENTRY - #128 (read a prior entry's displayed evidence as its full evidence), #131 (probe placed after an icall, reporting the previous iteration), and now #146. The pattern is always the same: a partial view of a small result set, treated as the whole. The rule that follows is concrete - when a probe fires a countable number of times, PRINT THEM ALL. `head` on an eleven-line result is not a summary, it is a sampling error.

[5] WHAT IS NOW ESTABLISHED. esi is already 0x00000004 and 0x00000017 on entry to the loc_00223738 block, so nothing in that block corrupts it - which also means #146's separate finding that sub_0020E5A0 preserves esi is still correct and still irrelevant. entries.claim: THE SMALL INTEGERS ARE CALLEE-SAVED CORRUPTION FROM THE TYPE-SETUP CALLBACKS, and it is SYSTEMIC rather than one bad call site. sub_002235D0 invokes a caller-supplied setup callback at loc_00223736 (the icall through MEM32(esp + 0x138), arg 8 per #116), and paired probes across that single call show FOUR of eleven callbacks failing to preserve esi: cb=002002B0 turns esi 01097498 into 00000004, cb=0021B890 turns 01098D08 into 00000017, cb=001F3370 turns 01098638 into 01098728, and cb=0021BB80 turns 010988F8 into 01098A68. The other seven - cb=001EA570, 00219A10, 0021BAC0 and four calls with cb=0 - preserve it correctly. The two corrupted-to-small-integer cases are exactly the values that later reach the free path and crash the boot.
entries.evidence:

Between them lies exactly one thing: `if (MEM32(esp + 0x13C) == 0) goto loc_00223738` else fall through loc_00223736's icall. So calls that skip the icall arrive clean and calls that take it can arrive corrupted.

[2] THE PAIRED MEASUREMENT, printed in full rather than sampled:
  PRE esi=01096BB8 cb=001EA570 -> POST 01096BB8    ok
  PRE esi=01091AB0 cb=00219A10 -> POST 01091AB0    ok
  PRE esi=01097858 cb=00000000 -> POST 01097858    ok (no call)
  PRE esi=010977C0 cb=00000000 -> POST 010977C0    ok

  PRE esi=01098638 cb=001F3370 -> POST 01098728    CLOBBERED
